weeks.title: Advanced Biomechanical Foundations
weeks.theme: Functional Anatomy, 3D Kinematics, Kinetics, the Kinetic Chain & Motor Control
weeks.question: What physical, mathematical and neuromotor principles must you command to tell what a pitching or hitting biomechanics measurement actually shows?

overview.text: Every claim in pitching and hitting biomechanics rests on a short list of physical and mathematical ideas: what a joint and a muscle–tendon unit can do, how a three-dimensional orientation is turned into three numbers, how forces and moments change motion, how a chain of segments produces speed at its end, and how a redundant nervous system organizes all of it. When those foundations are vague, reports are read as verdicts. When they are precise, the same reports become sets of measurements, assumptions and hypotheses that can be checked.

This week builds the foundations at graduate depth. Lesson 1 treats anatomy and muscle mechanics as constraints and asks how to tell a physical limitation from a coordination strategy or a task-specific adaptation. Lesson 2 is the mathematics of reference frames and rotation sequences, including why the same arm position can be reported with very different angles. Lesson 3 covers kinetics — impulse, moments, angular momentum, power and inverse dynamics — with worked numbers. Lesson 4 examines the kinetic chain and the evidence behind it. Lesson 5 introduces motor control: redundancy, variability and constraints.

Two habits run through every lesson. The first is to ask what kind of evidence stands behind a claim: a measurement, an association with a mechanical output such as ball or bat speed, an association with competitive outcomes, a demonstrated intervention effect, or retention and transfer of that effect. The second is the course's seven-question standard, applied each week to a specific claim. Most of the canonical findings you will meet are cross-sectional comparisons between athletes. They generate hypotheses about individuals; they do not prescribe changes.

lessons.title: Functional Anatomy & Physical Constraints
lessons.summary: Joint structure, muscle–tendon mechanics and physical capacity set the space of movements an athlete can produce; before calling a movement a fault, decide whether it reflects a physical limit, a coordination strategy or a task-specific adaptation.
objectives: Explain how glenohumeral, elbow, hip, thoracic and lead-knee structure constrain the movements used in pitching and hitting.
Apply force–length, force–velocity and series-elastic principles to predict how a muscle–tendon unit contributes to a fast movement.
Classify an observed movement difference as a physical limitation, a motor-control strategy or a task-specific adaptation, and state what evidence would distinguish them.
lessons.executive: Most mechanical 'faults' in a report are differences from a reference group. Some reflect what the athlete's body allows, some reflect how he has learned to organize it, and some are adaptations that throwing or hitting itself produced. These three explanations call for different decisions: a physical limitation calls for capacity work, a strategy may call for practice design or for no change, and an adaptation may be protective or performance-enhancing. The pitcher with less internal rotation in his throwing shoulder is the standard example: part of that difference is bone, built by years of throwing, and treating it as tightness to be stretched would misread the anatomy.

explore.text: Two right-handed pitchers in the same organization show the same number on a range-of-motion screen: about 20° less internal rotation in the throwing shoulder than in the other shoulder. One staff member recommends stretching both. A second says the number means nothing until you know the total arc and the bone. A third asks how each pitcher's external rotation at maximal layback compares with his passive range. All three have a point, and they are describing different mechanisms behind the same measurement. The case is hypothetical; the anatomy behind it is not.
Before reading on, write down three different explanations for a 20° side-to-side difference in passive shoulder internal rotation in a thrower. For each, name one measurement that would support it.

This lesson builds the anatomical and physiological vocabulary you need to answer that kind of question. It is not a review of anatomy you already know. It concentrates on the parts of structure and muscle mechanics that change how you read a biomechanics report: what a joint permits, how a muscle–tendon unit produces force at speed, why stretch before a fast movement matters, and how throwing itself remodels the skeleton.

understand.title: Prerequisite: degrees of freedom of a joint

blocks.text: A rigid body moving in space has six degrees of freedom: three translations and three rotations. A joint removes some of them. A hinge such as the humeroulnar joint allows essentially one rotation (flexion–extension); a ball-and-socket joint such as the glenohumeral or hip joint allows three rotations with small translations. When a report lists 'shoulder external rotation', 'abduction' and 'horizontal abduction', it is describing the three rotational degrees of freedom of one joint under one particular definition, which Lesson 2 takes apart.

understand.text: Joints that matter most in throwing and hitting

The **glenohumeral joint** is a shallow ball-and-socket joint whose stability depends heavily on the capsule, labrum and rotator cuff. Its large rotational range makes the extreme external rotation of the arm-cocking phase possible, and the same mobility means that large net loads must be controlled by soft tissue. Inverse-dynamics studies of skilled pitchers report large net internal-rotation and varus moments around maximal external rotation and large compressive forces near release, which is why those instants dominate discussions of loading ([Fleisig et al., 1995](R-fleisig-1995-kinetics); [Winter, 2009](R-winter-2009-biomechanics)).

The **elbow** combines the humeroulnar hinge, the humeroradial joint and the proximal radioulnar joint. In throwing, the forearm lags behind the upper arm as the humerus rotates, which loads the medial side of the elbow in valgus; the net varus moment computed by inverse dynamics is the summed internal response to that load from all structures crossing the joint ([Fleisig et al., 1995](R-fleisig-1995-kinetics)). The **hip** is a deep ball-and-socket joint whose internal and external rotation, together with pelvis orientation, determines how the pelvis can rotate over a fixed lead leg in both pitching and hitting. The **thoracic spine and rib cage** contribute rotation, lateral flexion and extension that change trunk orientation and therefore the orientation of the shoulder girdle in space. The **lead knee** acts as the pivot of a rotating, decelerating body: in pitching, how the lead knee flexes or extends after foot contact differs between groups of pitchers who throw at different velocities ([Matsuo et al., 2001](R-matsuo-2001-comparison)).
Muscle–tendon mechanics

Three relationships govern what a muscle–tendon unit can do. The **force–length relationship** says that isometric force depends on sarcomere length, with maximal active force over a middle range and less at very short or very long lengths, while passive tissue adds force at long lengths. The **force–velocity relationship** says that a shortening muscle produces less force the faster it shortens, and a lengthening muscle can produce more than its isometric maximum. **Architecture** — fibre length, pennation and physiological cross-sectional area — sets these curves for a given muscle: cross-sectional area mainly determines maximal force, while the number of sarcomeres in series determines excursion and maximal shortening velocity ([Lieber and Fridén, 2000](R-lieber-2000-functional); [Winter, 2009](R-winter-2009-biomechanics)).

A worked consequence. Hill-type models describe the shortening branch as (F + a)(v + b) = constant. With a common normalization in which a/F0 is about 0.25, the force at one third of maximal shortening velocity is about 0.29 of isometric maximum, and mechanical power peaks near 0.31 of maximal velocity at roughly 0.095 × F0 × Vmax. The practical meaning: a muscle shortening very fast contributes little force and little power. The extreme segment velocities in throwing and swinging therefore cannot be explained by muscles shortening at those speeds alone; they need other mechanisms, chiefly elastic recoil and segment interaction (Lesson 3).

understand.caption: Force and power on the shortening branch of a Hill-type curve (a/F0 = 0.25)
understand.note: Computed from the normalized Hill equation F/F0 = (1 − v/Vmax) / (1 + (v/Vmax)/0.25). Illustrative parameter; real muscles vary with fibre type and temperature.

understand.text: Series elasticity and elastic energy

Tendons, aponeuroses and other passive tissues act in series with the contractile elements. When a joint is driven into a stretch while muscles resist, these tissues lengthen and store elastic strain energy that can be returned during the subsequent shortening, faster than the contractile element could deliver it alone. Roach and colleagues measured 20 experienced throwers and argued that during arm cocking the shoulder's soft tissues store elastic energy that powers the very rapid humeral internal rotation that follows; restricting external rotation with a brace reduced work and power at the elbow, consistent with that account ([Roach et al., 2013](R-roach-2013-elastic)).
Task-specific adaptation: humeral retroversion

The throwing arm itself changes with years of throwing. Computed tomography of professional pitchers showed more humeral head retroversion on the throwing side than on the non-throwing side, along with more external rotation and less internal rotation, while the total arc of rotation was similar between sides ([Crockett et al., 2002](R-crockett-2002-osseous)). At least part of the rotation 'deficit' is therefore a shift of the arc produced by bone shape, not tightness. Range-of-motion screening has to be read with that in mind.
Anthropometric and capacity constraints

Segment lengths, masses and moments of inertia are physical constraints that no coaching cue changes. For a point on a rotating segment, linear speed equals angular velocity times radius (v = ωr), so a longer lever produces more endpoint speed for the same angular velocity; but the segment's moment of inertia grows with mass times the square of distance, so the same lever needs more moment to accelerate. Laboratories estimate these inertial parameters from regression tables or scaling rules rather than measuring them on each athlete, which adds error to every computed moment ([Winter, 2009](R-winter-2009-biomechanics); [Robertson et al., 2014](R-robertson-2014-research)).

A worked comparison. If the forearm and hand rotate about the elbow at 40 rad/s, a point 0.30 m from the elbow moves at 12 m/s and a point 0.35 m away at 14 m/s. Taller athletes are not automatically faster throwers or swingers, however: a longer, heavier segment is harder to accelerate, and strength, tissue properties and coordination must scale with it. Physical capacity — strength, rate of force development, mobility and tissue tolerance — is the other half of the constraint. It sets how large the moments and powers can be, and how much load the tissues can repeatedly absorb. Capacity is trainable but slowly, and its relationship to on-field mechanics runs through coordination rather than directly.

understand.caption: Three explanations for the same movement difference
y: Not produced by the task itself
Produced or shaped by the task itself
cells: Physical limitation: structure or capacity sets a boundary (bone geometry from another cause, a strength deficit, a prior injury)
Motor-control strategy: the body permits alternatives, and the athlete has learned or chosen one of them
Task-specific adaptation: years of the task changed structure (humeral retroversion; side-to-side differences in rotation)
Adaptive strategy: a learned solution that exploits the athlete's own anatomy, such as a slot that fits his shoulder
understand.note: Teaching device. Boundaries are fuzzy: strength is trainable but slowly; adaptations can be partly reversible. The point is to ask which explanation the evidence supports before choosing an intervention.

understand.title: Methodological note: why a net joint moment says little about one muscle

blocks.text: Inverse dynamics returns a single net moment about each joint axis. That value is the algebraic sum of moments from all muscles, ligaments, joint capsule and bony contact acting at that instant. Co-contraction raises internal muscle forces without changing the net moment; passive tissue can carry load that a muscle-based reading would assign to a muscle. Partitioning the net moment among structures requires a musculoskeletal model with its own assumptions ([Winter, 2009](R-winter-2009-biomechanics); [Zajac and Gordon, 1989](R-zajac-1989-determining)).

challenge.text: Where the anatomy argument gets overstated

Range-of-motion differences are often treated as injury risk factors. The evidence is mixed. In a prospective study of professional pitchers measured over three seasons, pitchers with an internal-rotation deficit were nearly twice as likely to be injured, but the difference was not statistically significant; a deficit in total rotational motion greater than 5° was associated with more injuries ([Wilk et al., 2011](R-wilk-2011-correlation)). A systematic review of pitching mechanics and injury found that low power and a lack of prospective three-dimensional studies prevent most mechanical variables from being established as risk factors ([Bullock et al., 2021](R-bullock-2021-baseball)). The bony adaptation evidence suggests that some of the internal-rotation loss is expected rather than pathological ([Crockett et al., 2002](R-crockett-2002-osseous)).

The elastic-energy account is also easier to state than to quantify. Roach and colleagues inferred storage from a model and a bracing manipulation in non-elite throwers; how much of an elite pitcher's arm speed comes from stored energy, and whether training can increase it safely, is not established ([Roach et al., 2013](R-roach-2013-elastic)). Their evolutionary inference — that throwing shaped early Homo — is a separate claim that some anthropologists dispute. Meanwhile, the induced-acceleration evidence attributes much of distal segment velocity to velocity-dependent interaction torques rather than to any one tissue ([Hirashima et al., 2008](R-hirashima-2008-kinetic)). These accounts are compatible, but they compete for the same velocity budget, and the shares are unknown.

challenge.caption: The seven-question standard applied to a claim: “Greater layback (maximal shoulder external rotation) makes a pitcher throw harder.”
rows: Between-pitcher comparisons show greater maximal external rotation in a high-velocity group than in a low-velocity group ([Matsuo et al., 2001](R-matsuo-2001-comparison)). That is a biomechanical measurement (category 1) associated with a mechanical output, ball speed (category 2).
A longer acceleration path for the hand, plus elastic storage in stretched shoulder tissues that is returned during internal rotation ([Roach et al., 2013](R-roach-2013-elastic)).
Cross-sectional group differences and a small laboratory manipulation (bracing reduced downstream work and power). No randomized study increases layback and measures velocity.
How much of the association reflects passive range, bone geometry, strength or timing; whether the same relationship holds within a pitcher; the dose–response shape.
Has changing the variable improved performance?
Not demonstrated. No intervention study shows that training greater layback raises velocity (category 4 is empty).
Does the improvement transfer to competition?
Unknown. There is no evidence linking a layback change to competitive outcomes (categories 3 and 5 are empty).
What are the implications for loading or potential injury-related risk?

Greater external rotation coincides with large net internal-rotation and varus moments near that instant ([Fleisig et al., 1995](R-fleisig-1995-kinetics)). A net moment is not an injury probability, but the claim cannot be judged on velocity alone.

apply.text: Worked problem: reading a range-of-motion screen

Hypothetical data. A right-handed pitcher has passive internal rotation of 45° on the throwing side and 65° on the other side; external rotation is 120° on the throwing side and 100° on the other. Internal rotation differs by 20°. Total arc is 45 + 120 = 165° on the throwing side and 65 + 100 = 165° on the other: no total-arc deficit. The arc has shifted toward external rotation, a pattern consistent with humeral retroversion and with the professional data, not with global tightness.

Change one number: suppose throwing-side external rotation were 105°. Total arc would be 150° against 165°, a 15° total-arc deficit. Now the side-to-side pattern differs from the expected adaptation, and the association with injury reported for total-arc deficits becomes relevant — as a reason for clinical evaluation, not as a diagnosis ([Wilk et al., 2011](R-wilk-2011-correlation)). Note the measurement problem as well: goniometry has errors of several degrees, so a 5° threshold sits close to measurement noise (Week 2).

For hitting, the same reasoning applies to hip rotation. A hitter who cannot internally rotate the lead hip far may stop pelvis rotation early and finish with the trunk alone. Whether that is a structural limit, a strength limit or a learned pattern changes the plan: imaging and clinical assessment for the first, capacity work for the second, practice design for the third. A swing difference by itself does not say which.

apply.title: Executive twist: one screen, three departments

blocks.text: Your medical staff, strength staff and pitching coaches each read the same range-of-motion screen. Medical sees a possible risk factor, strength sees a mobility target and coaching sees a slot. With incomplete evidence, the defensible decision rule is to agree in advance which pattern triggers which referral, to read total arc and side-to-side differences rather than one number, and to treat bone-driven shifts as normal for throwers unless a clinician says otherwise. The clinical judgement belongs to licensed clinicians; your role is to make sure the data reach them in interpretable form.

retain.text: Structure, muscle mechanics and adaptation set the space of movements an athlete can use. Muscles shortening fast produce little force, so the fastest segment motions in baseball depend on elastic recoil and segment interaction. A movement difference may be a limitation, a strategy or an adaptation, and only additional evidence distinguishes them.
Why does force–velocity mean that elastic recoil and segment interaction are needed to explain humeral internal rotation velocity in pitching?
A thrower has 20° less internal rotation on the throwing side but the same total arc. What does that pattern suggest, and what does it not tell you?
Give one example each of a physical limitation, a strategy and a task-specific adaptation in hitting.

Force–velocity limits mean that the fastest motions in throwing depend on elastic storage and segment interaction, not muscle shortening speed alone.
Throwers' humeri are more retroverted on the throwing side; part of the internal-rotation 'deficit' is expected bony adaptation.
Range-of-motion associations with injury are mixed and should be read through total arc and measurement error.

check.prompt: A professional pitcher's throwing shoulder shows 20° less internal rotation and 20° more external rotation than his non-throwing shoulder. Which interpretation is best supported by the evidence in this lesson?

options.text: The shoulder is tight and needs stretching until internal rotation matches the other side.
The arc has shifted, a pattern consistent with throwing-related humeral retroversion; total arc is preserved.
He has a total-arc deficit and is at high injury risk.
The difference is measurement error because goniometers are unreliable.

check.explanation: Equal and opposite changes leave the total arc unchanged, which matches the pattern reported in professional pitchers with greater humeral retroversion on the throwing side. That does not rule out other problems, but it is the expected adaptation rather than evidence of tightness or a total-arc deficit.

optionFeedback.a: Part of the shift is bony; stretching does not change bone geometry, and the total arc is normal.
optionFeedback.c: Total arc is the same on both sides here, so there is no total-arc deficit.
optionFeedback.d: Goniometric error is several degrees, not 20° in both directions at once.

check.prompt: Using the normalized Hill relationship F/F0 = (1 − v/Vmax) / (1 + (v/Vmax)/0.25), what fraction of isometric maximum force does the muscle produce when shortening at half its maximal velocity? Give a decimal to two places.
check.working: v/Vmax = 0.5. Numerator 1 − 0.5 = 0.5. Denominator 1 + 0.5/0.25 = 1 + 2 = 3. F/F0 = 0.5/3 ≈ 0.167, which rounds to 0.17.
check.explanation: At half of maximal shortening velocity this Hill-type muscle produces only about 17% of its isometric force. Fast shortening is weak shortening, which is why fast throwing and swinging motions depend on elastic recoil and segment interaction as well as muscle.

lessons.title: Three-Dimensional Human Movement: Frames, Rotations and Joint Angles
lessons.summary: A 3D joint angle is not a property of the body alone; it is the output of a chosen reference frame and a chosen rotation sequence, and the same orientation can be reported with materially different numbers.
objectives: Distinguish global (laboratory) and segment-fixed reference frames and compute how a segment's orientation is reported relative to each.
Explain Euler and Cardan sequences, the ISB conventions for the shoulder, and why gimbal lock occurs.
Interpret two reported shoulder angles and decide whether they are comparable.
lessons.executive: When two reports disagree about a pitcher's shoulder abduction or a hitter's trunk rotation, the first question is not who measured better but whether they measured the same thing. A three-dimensional joint angle depends on how each segment's axes are defined, which segment is the reference, and the order in which three rotations are extracted. The same arm position can be reported as 60°, 71° or 119° of axial rotation depending on the sequence. Comparing numbers across vendors, laboratories or seasons without matching definitions produces errors larger than most of the changes coaches care about.

explore.text: A hypothetical pitcher is captured by two systems on consecutive days. One reports 165° of maximal shoulder external rotation; the other reports 178°. The coaching staff asks which system is wrong. Both could be correct, and the pitcher could have thrown identically on both days. The systems might define the trunk segment differently, use different rotation sequences, or report external rotation relative to the trunk in one case and to a modified humeral frame in the other.

Predict: if you hold your right arm out to the side at shoulder height and then rotate it so your palm faces forward, how many distinct ways can you think of to describe that position in three numbers?

This lesson gives you the mathematics to answer that question exactly. It is the most technical lesson of the week, and it pays off every time you read a joint angle in a report, compare a vendor's output with a laboratory's, or ask whether a change across seasons is real.

understand.title: Prerequisite: vectors, axes and the right-hand rule

blocks.text: A reference frame is an origin plus three mutually perpendicular unit vectors. In this course, the laboratory frame has X pointing anteriorly (toward home plate for a pitcher), Y pointing vertically up and Z pointing to the right, which forms a right-handed set: X × Y = Z. A positive rotation about an axis follows the right-hand rule: point the right thumb along the axis and the fingers curl in the positive direction. Every sign in a joint-angle report depends on these choices, so a report that does not state them cannot be fully interpreted.

understand.text: Global and segment-fixed frames

A **global** or laboratory frame is fixed to the ground. A **segment-fixed** frame is attached to a body segment and moves with it; it is built from anatomical landmarks (for the thorax, for example, from the sternum, spinous processes and the C7 and T8 vertebrae). A **joint angle** describes the orientation of one segment-fixed frame relative to another — the humerus relative to the thorax, the pelvis relative to the femur. A **segment angle** describes a segment relative to the laboratory. The ISB recommendations specify landmarks and axes for each segment so that laboratories can compare results ([Wu et al., 2002](R-wu-2002-isb); [Wu et al., 2005](R-wu-2005-isb)).

Worked example in the frontal plane. A pitcher's trunk is tilted 30° toward the glove side at release, and his humerus is abducted 90° relative to the trunk. Relative to the laboratory, the arm is then 120° from the downward vertical, or 30° above horizontal. A coach looking at video sees a high arm slot; a joint-angle report says the shoulder is at an ordinary 90° of abduction. Both descriptions are correct. The slot comes mostly from the trunk, not from the shoulder — which is why trunk tilt and arm slot are studied together ([Oyama et al., 2013](R-oyama-2013-effect)).
Translation, rotation and their rates

A segment's motion combines translation of a reference point (usually its centre of mass) and rotation about that point. Linear velocity is the rate of change of position (m/s) and linear acceleration its rate of change (m/s²). Angular velocity ω is the rate of rotation (rad/s), and angular acceleration α its rate of change (rad/s²). For a point at position r from a rotation axis, the velocity due to rotation is ω × r, perpendicular to both; the total velocity of a point on a moving segment is the velocity of the reference point plus ω × r. This is why bat-head speed depends both on how fast the hands translate and on how fast the bat rotates about them ([Winter, 2009](R-winter-2009-biomechanics); [Robertson et al., 2014](R-robertson-2014-research)).

A short numeric illustration. If the hands move forward at 8 m/s and the bat rotates about them at 30 rad/s, a point on the barrel 0.6 m from the hands gains 18 m/s from rotation. When the rotational contribution is aligned with the hands' velocity, the barrel point moves at about 26 m/s; when it is not, the vector sum is smaller. Speeds alone, without directions, cannot be added. Angular acceleration matters as well: a segment can reach the same peak angular velocity with a short, intense acceleration or a long, gentle one, and the two have different kinetic demands.
Rotations do not commute

Orientation in three dimensions needs three numbers, but unlike translations, rotations do not commute: rotating 90° about X and then 90° about Y produces a different orientation from rotating about Y and then X. To report an orientation as three angles, you must choose a **sequence**. **Cardan** (Tait–Bryan) sequences use three different axes (for example Z–X–Y); **proper Euler** sequences repeat the first axis (Y–X–Y). Each sequence is a valid description of the same orientation; the three angles it returns differ from those of other sequences ([Robertson et al., 2014](R-robertson-2014-research); [Winter, 2009](R-winter-2009-biomechanics)).

Grood and Suntay's joint coordinate system defines the first axis in the proximal segment, the third axis in the distal segment and a floating axis perpendicular to both; the description it yields is equivalent to a particular Cardan sequence and became the basis of the ISB recommendations ([Grood and Suntay, 1983](R-grood-1983-joint)). For the humerus relative to the thorax, the ISB recommends a Y–X–Y Euler sequence: plane of elevation, elevation, then axial rotation ([Wu et al., 2005](R-wu-2005-isb)).
Flagship example: one orientation, three sets of angles

Take a right humerus elevated 70° from the side of the thorax in a plane 30° anterior to the frontal plane, and rotated +60° about its own long axis (right-hand rule about the humeral Y axis, which points from the elbow toward the shoulder). Build the rotation matrix from that description and then decompose the same matrix under three sequences, with angles measured about the mobile axes. The table shows the results, computed and checked by reconstructing the matrix from each set of angles.

understand.caption: The same humerus-relative-to-thorax orientation reported under three sequences
understand.note: Original computation, checked by rebuilding the matrix from each row. Frames: X anterior, Y superior, Z right; rotations about mobile axes; magnitudes shown, signs depend on stated conventions. Every sequence has two equivalent solutions: for Z–X–Y the one with the middle angle between −90° and +90° is shown; for Y–X–Y the same orientation can also be written (−150°, +70°, −120°), the branch with positive elevation that the week laboratory displays.

understand.text: Nothing about the arm changed between rows. 'Abduction' is 67° under one sequence and 55° under another; axial rotation is 60°, 71° or 119°. A difference of that size between two reports is entirely definitional. Even within one sequence the description is not unique: each orientation has two equivalent sets of angles, and software must pick a branch, so a plane of elevation of 30° in one program can appear as −150° in another. This is why the first question about any shoulder value is: relative to which segment, with which axes, under which sequence and branch?
Gimbal lock

Every three-angle sequence has orientations at which it becomes singular. For a Cardan sequence, this happens when the middle rotation reaches ±90°: the first and third axes line up, only their sum or difference is defined, and small changes in orientation produce large, erratic jumps in the reported angles. For a proper Euler sequence such as Y–X–Y, the singularity is at a middle angle of 0° or 180° — for the ISB shoulder sequence, with the arm hanging at the side. Shoulder studies show that the choice of sequence changes reported angles and that sequences should be chosen to keep the task away from their singularities ([Šenk and Chèze, 2006](R-senk-2006-rotation); [Wu et al., 2005](R-wu-2005-isb)).

In pitching this is not a theoretical concern. At foot contact the humerus is often near 90° of abduction relative to the trunk — exactly where a Z–X–Y (flexion, abduction, rotation) sequence locks. A system using that sequence can report wildly oscillating horizontal abduction and external rotation for a pitcher whose arm is moving smoothly. Laboratories handle this by choosing a different sequence for the throwing shoulder, by redefining the humeral frame, or by reporting angles only in parts of the motion where the sequence is stable. The report should say which.

understand.title: Methodological note: angular velocity is not the derivative of a joint angle

blocks.text: A segment's angular velocity is a vector, ω. For planar motion about one fixed axis, ω equals the time derivative of the angle. In three dimensions it does not: ω is the sum of the three Euler-angle rates, each multiplied by its own axis, and those axes move. Differentiating a reported 'shoulder external rotation' curve therefore does not give the angular velocity about the humeral long axis except in special cases. Many pitching reports compute angular velocity directly from segment orientations, which is correct, while others differentiate angles; the methods section is where you find out ([Robertson et al., 2014](R-robertson-2014-research)).

Unit conversion is the other recurring trap. Reports quote angular velocity in degrees per second; physics formulas use radians per second. One radian is 180/π ≈ 57.3°, so a pelvis rotating at 600°/s is turning at about 10.5 rad/s, and a hand 0.6 m from the rotation axis would move at about 6.3 m/s from that rotation alone.

challenge.text: Standards versus practice

The ISB recommendation is a consensus, not a proof. The Y–X–Y shoulder sequence is clinically intuitive at high elevation but singular with the arm at the side, and it is not the sequence many baseball laboratories use for the throwing shoulder. Shoulder research shows that sequence choice changes the angles enough to alter interpretation and argues for choosing it by task ([Šenk and Chèze, 2006](R-senk-2006-rotation)); the ISB authors themselves acknowledge alternatives ([Wu et al., 2005](R-wu-2005-isb)). In practice, reports from different systems are often not comparable even when the variable names match.

Definitions also differ upstream of the sequence. Where the trunk segment begins and ends, whether pelvis rotation is measured relative to the laboratory or to the line toward home plate, and whether shoulder angles are relative to the thorax or to the scapula all change the numbers. Markerless systems estimate joint centres from images rather than from palpated landmarks, which shifts axes and therefore angles; this is a Week 2 topic, but its root is here.

challenge.caption: The seven-question standard applied to a claim: “A shoulder abduction below 90° at foot contact is a mechanical flaw that should be corrected.”
rows: A reported angle at one event, usually compared with group averages. It is a biomechanical measurement (category 1) whose value depends on frame and sequence.
Usually unstated; sometimes that a lower arm position changes elbow loading or arm path timing.
Group-average angles from laboratory samples; little or no evidence links this specific threshold to ball speed within pitchers, and none to competitive outcomes.
Whether the value was computed under a sequence that is singular near 90°; whether the same pitcher's value is stable across trials; whether the threshold applies to his trunk tilt and slot.
Has changing the variable improved performance?
Not shown. No intervention study demonstrates that raising abduction at foot contact improves velocity or command.
Does the improvement transfer to competition?
What are the implications for loading or potential injury-related risk?
Abduction at an event is not a load. Any loading claim would need kinetics, and even then a net moment is not an injury probability.

apply.text: Worked interpretation: two reports, one pitcher

Hypothetical reports. System A reports maximal shoulder external rotation of 165° using humerus relative to thorax with a sequence chosen to avoid singularity near 90° abduction. System B reports 178° but defines external rotation relative to the trunk segment built from shoulder and hip joint centres. Before comparing the 13° difference with anything, you would ask: Are the trunk segments defined the same way? Is external rotation measured about the same humeral axis? Which sequence? Are both values from the same pitches? If the answers differ, the 13° is a definitional offset and the two systems' values need separate norms.

For hitting, the same logic applies to 'hip–shoulder separation'. One system computes the angle between pelvis and upper-trunk segment orientations projected onto the horizontal plane; another computes a three-dimensional relative rotation about the trunk's long axis. When the trunk is flexed and tilted at foot plant, the projected and the three-dimensional values can differ by many degrees. A hitting coach comparing a hitter's number to a published norm must know which one both use.

blocks.text: If your organization changes capture systems, last season's values and this season's cannot be placed on the same chart without a bridging study: the same athletes captured by both systems, with the offset and agreement estimated for each variable. Without it, a 'change' across the switch is uninterpretable. Budget for the overlap period, and require written definitions (segment frames, sequences, event detection) as a condition of any contract.

retain.text: A 3D joint angle is a description chosen by the analyst: a reference segment, a set of axes and a rotation sequence. The same orientation can produce very different numbers under different sequences, and every sequence has singular orientations where values become unstable. Compare angles only when definitions match.
Why can two correct systems report different shoulder external rotation for the same pitch?
At what middle-angle values do Cardan and proper Euler sequences lock, and why does that matter for a throwing shoulder near 90° abduction?
A pitcher's trunk tilts 25° toward the glove side and his humerus is abducted 90° relative to the trunk. How far above horizontal is the arm in the laboratory frame?

lessons.title: Kinetics: Forces, Moments, Momentum and Power
lessons.summary: Forces change linear momentum, moments change angular momentum, and inverse dynamics turns motion into net joint moments and powers — numbers that are net, model-dependent and never loads on a single tissue.
objectives: Apply Newton's laws, impulse–momentum and angular impulse–momentum to segment and whole-body problems with correct units and signs.
Compute a moment as r × F and a joint power as moment times angular velocity, and interpret their signs.
Explain what inverse dynamics assumes and why a net joint moment is not a muscle, ligament or injury measure.
lessons.executive: Kinetics is the part of a biomechanics report most likely to be over-read. Ground reaction forces and impulses are measured; joint moments, joint forces and powers are computed from motion, estimated segment properties and the forces at the feet. They are net quantities summed over every structure at a joint, so an elbow varus moment is not the load on the ulnar collateral ligament, and a larger moment is not a measured probability of injury. Kinetics remains the right language for asking how a delivery or swing produces speed, and for comparing a player with himself under consistent methods.

explore.text: Hypothetical scenario. A force-plate report shows that one hitter's lead leg produces a higher peak vertical ground reaction force than another's, and a staff member concludes that the first hitter is 'using the ground better'. Peak force alone does not establish that. What changes the body's momentum is impulse — force integrated over time — net of body weight, and in the direction that matters for the task. A brief, high peak can produce less impulse than a lower, longer push.

Before reading on: a pitcher's lead leg produces a braking force that rises to 1,200 N in 0.05 s and falls back to zero 0.10 s later. What single number would you want to know to say how much it slowed his forward motion, and how would you get it?

understand.title: Prerequisite: Newton's laws for a segment

blocks.text: Newton's second law for a segment is ΣF = m·a_cm: the sum of external forces equals mass times the acceleration of the centre of mass. Its rotational counterpart about the centre of mass is ΣM = dL/dt, where L is angular momentum; for rotation about a single fixed axis this reduces to ΣM = I·α. The third law says that the force segment A exerts on segment B is equal and opposite to the force B exerts on A, which is what lets inverse dynamics pass forces from one segment to the next ([Winter, 2009](R-winter-2009-biomechanics)).

understand.text: Impulse and momentum

Integrating Newton's second law over time gives the impulse–momentum relationship: ∫F dt = Δ(m·v). Impulse is the area under a force–time curve, in newton-seconds. Ground reaction forces are measured directly with force plates; the impulse they deliver, minus the impulse of gravity in the vertical direction, determines the change in the body's linear momentum ([Winter, 2009](R-winter-2009-biomechanics); [Robertson et al., 2014](R-robertson-2014-research)).

Worked example. The braking force in the prompt rises linearly to 1,200 N over 0.05 s and falls linearly to zero over the next 0.10 s, a triangle with base 0.15 s. Its impulse is ½ × 1,200 N × 0.15 s = 90 N·s. If this is the net horizontal force on a 90 kg pitcher, his centre of mass slows by 90/90 = 1.0 m/s. Doubling the peak while halving the duration gives the same impulse and the same change in velocity. For vertical forces, subtract body weight first: a 90 kg athlete weighs about 883 N, and only the force above that changes vertical momentum.
Moments

A force that does not pass through an axis produces a **moment** (torque) about it: M = r × F, where r runs from the axis to the point where the force acts. The magnitude is |r|·|F|·sin θ, equivalently the force times its perpendicular distance from the axis (the **moment arm**), and the direction follows the right-hand rule ([Winter, 2009](R-winter-2009-biomechanics)).

Two worked examples. First, a 400 N muscle force acting 0.05 m from a joint centre produces 400 × 0.05 = 20 N·m. Second, in vector form, a force F = (0, 0, 200) N applied at r = (0.30, 0, 0) m from the axis gives r × F = (0·200 − 0·0, 0·0 − 0.30·200, 0.30·0 − 0·0) = (0, −60, 0) N·m: a 60 N·m moment about the negative Y axis. Swap the order to F × r and the sign flips, which is one reason reports disagree about whether a moment is 'positive'. Always check the stated convention.
Angular momentum and angular impulse

Angular momentum L of a rigid segment about its centre of mass is I·ω for rotation about a principal axis, where I is the moment of inertia (kg·m²). For a system of segments, total angular momentum about the whole-body centre of mass changes only through external moments, chiefly those of the ground reaction forces. Internal muscle moments can redistribute angular momentum among segments but cannot change the total. Angular impulse, the time integral of moment, equals the change in angular momentum ([Winter, 2009](R-winter-2009-biomechanics)).

Worked example. An average net moment of 50 N·m acting for 0.08 s delivers an angular impulse of 4 N·m·s. Applied to a segment with I = 0.2 kg·m² about its axis, it changes angular velocity by 4/0.2 = 20 rad/s, about 1,150°/s. The same angular impulse applied to a segment ten times heavier in rotational terms changes its angular velocity by one tenth as much. This is the arithmetic behind the intuition that big segments are slow to start and small segments can be made very fast.

The whole-body version matters for both skills. During the stride and the swing, the only significant external forces are gravity and the ground reaction forces under the feet. Gravity acts at the centre of mass and produces no moment about it, so every change in the body's total angular momentum about its centre of mass comes from ground reaction forces whose lines of action miss the centre of mass. A hitter who braces on the lead leg with the force passing in front of his centre of mass generates angular momentum about a vertical-ish axis; the arms, bat and trunk then share and redistribute that momentum through internal moments. Where the trunk's rotation 'comes from' is therefore partly a question about the feet.
Mechanical power and energy

Joint power is the product of the net joint moment and the joint angular velocity, P = M·ω. Positive power means the moment acts in the direction of rotation and generates mechanical energy; negative power means it opposes the rotation and absorbs energy. Segment energy is the sum of translational kinetic, rotational kinetic and potential energy. Power can also be transferred between adjacent segments through joint forces, which do no net work on the pair but move energy from one segment to the other ([Winter, 2009](R-winter-2009-biomechanics)).

A shoulder internal-rotation moment of 60 N·m acting while the humerus internally rotates at 40 rad/s generates 2,400 W at that instant. The same moment acting during external rotation, against the motion, absorbs energy: −2,400 W. During arm cocking the internal-rotation moment opposes external rotation; during acceleration it acts with internal rotation. The sign change is the mechanical signature of the decelerate-then-accelerate pattern discussed in Lesson 1.
Inverse dynamics

steps.label: Motion data
steps.text: Marker or markerless trajectories, filtered, define segment frames and their linear and angular accelerations.

steps.label: Segment parameters
steps.text: Mass, centre-of-mass location and moments of inertia estimated from tables or scaling.

steps.label: External forces
steps.text: Ground reaction forces from force plates, or an assumption such as zero force at a free hand.

steps.label: Equations of motion
steps.text: Newton–Euler equations solved segment by segment from the distal end inward.

steps.label: Net joint forces and moments
steps.text: Resultants at each joint, expressed in a chosen frame and often normalized to body size.

understand.text: The net moment combines every structure crossing the joint. Co-contraction raises tissue loads without raising the net moment, and ligaments and joint contact can carry load that the net value hides. Results depend on filtering (high-speed throwing data are very sensitive to cut-off frequency), segment parameters, joint-centre locations and the frame in which moments are expressed ([Winter, 2009](R-winter-2009-biomechanics); [Fleisig et al., 1995](R-fleisig-1995-kinetics)).

understand.title: Methodological note: interaction torques

blocks.text: In a chain of linked segments, the motion of one segment produces moments on its neighbours even with no muscle activity at the joint between them. For a two-segment arm, the equation for the distal joint contains terms proportional to the proximal segment's angular acceleration and to the square of its angular velocity. These velocity-dependent **interaction torques** let a rapidly rotating trunk and upper arm whip the forearm. Muscles therefore accelerate joints they do not cross, and can even oppose their anatomical action at joints they do cross ([Zajac and Gordon, 1989](R-zajac-1989-determining); [Putnam, 1993](R-putnam-1993-sequential)). Induced-acceleration analysis of throwing attributes much of elbow extension and wrist flexion velocity near release to such velocity-dependent effects arising from trunk rotation and shoulder internal rotation ([Hirashima et al., 2008](R-hirashima-2008-kinetic)).

challenge.text: What kinetics cannot tell you

Pitching kinetics were developed partly to explain injury, and the moments at maximal external rotation are described as large enough to approach tissue failure limits in cadaveric testing ([Fleisig et al., 1995](R-fleisig-1995-kinetics)). The prospective evidence connecting computed moments to injury is thin: a systematic review found elbow valgus torque among the few variables with support, but noted low power and no prospective three-dimensional studies ([Bullock et al., 2021](R-bullock-2021-baseball)). Normalized moments also rise with ball velocity, both across and within pitchers ([Stodden et al., 2005](R-stodden-2005-relationship)), so 'high torque' and 'high velocity' are not independent findings.

Two technical issues make published kinetic values less portable than they look. The first is filtering. Joint moments depend on accelerations, which are second derivatives of noisy position data; the cut-off frequency chosen for marker data and for force data changes peak moments, and filtering the two differently can create artificial peaks near foot contact or ball release. The second is normalization. Moments are often divided by body weight times height to compare athletes of different sizes, but that assumes loads scale linearly with size, and it does nothing to remove the dependence on velocity. A pitcher who throws harder will usually show larger normalized moments, so comparing him with slower pitchers on a percentile chart mixes skill, size and load.

challenge.caption: The seven-question standard applied to a claim: “This pitcher's elbow varus moment of 100 N·m means his UCL is at high risk.”
rows: A net varus moment computed by inverse dynamics on a set of pitches (a biomechanical measurement, category 1).
The UCL resists valgus load; a larger net varus moment implies a larger valgus load to be resisted by all medial structures.

Cadaveric failure data and a small number of prospective or retrospective studies; the systematic review supports valgus torque as a risk factor only provisionally ([Bullock et al., 2021](R-bullock-2021-baseball)).
How load is shared among ligament, muscle and bone; tissue capacity of this individual; the cumulative workload; model and filtering error in the 100 N·m estimate.
Has changing the variable improved performance?
Reducing the moment by mechanical change has not been shown to reduce injury in a controlled study.
Does the improvement transfer to competition?
Not applicable as stated; if reductions also lower velocity, competitive cost must be considered.
What are the implications for loading or potential injury-related risk?
The value is a load indicator, not a probability. It is useful for comparing the same pitcher under consistent methods and for clinical discussion, within clinical boundaries.

apply.text: Worked problem: reading a kinetics table

Synthetic data. A report lists, for one pitcher, elbow varus moment 88 N·m (4.6 %BW×H), shoulder internal-rotation moment 90 N·m and peak lead-leg vertical ground reaction force 1.9 × body weight. Three questions come before any interpretation. Were these averaged over several fastballs or taken from one? Which filter cut-off and segment model were used, and are they the same as in the comparison data? Are the moments expressed in the distal or proximal segment frame? Only then can you ask whether 88 N·m is high for this pitcher relative to his own history at similar velocity.

A second synthetic calculation. A 90 kg hitter's lead-leg vertical force averages 1,500 N over a 0.12 s window during the swing. Body weight is about 883 N, but his rear leg is also on the ground carrying some of it, so the impulse of the lead leg alone does not determine whole-body vertical momentum. If both legs together average 1,300 N over that window, the net vertical impulse is (1,300 − 883) × 0.12 ≈ 50 N·s, an upward velocity change of about 0.56 m/s. The lesson for reports: impulses must be summed over every contact and net of gravity before they say anything about the centre of mass.

For hitting, the analogous kinetic questions concern the lead leg and the trunk. A higher lead-leg braking impulse slows the body's forward motion, and the change in the body's linear momentum can be redirected into rotation about the lead side. Whether a particular hitter benefits from more braking depends on his timing and his bat path, and the evidence for prescribing it is associational (Lesson 4).

blocks.text: A vendor offers a dashboard that colours each pitcher's elbow moment red above a league percentile. Before adopting it, ask whether the moments were computed with the same model as the reference population, whether they are normalized for size and velocity, and what decision a red flag triggers. A defensible use is within-pitcher monitoring with consistent methods and clinical review; an indefensible use is labelling a pitcher high-risk from a single between-pitcher percentile.

retain.text: Impulse changes momentum; angular impulse changes angular momentum; power is moment times angular velocity. Inverse dynamics turns motion into net joint moments that are model-dependent and summed over every structure at the joint. Interaction torques mean that muscles affect joints they do not cross.

lessons.title: The Kinetic Chain in Baseball: Sequencing, Energy Flow and Evidence
lessons.summary: Proximal-to-distal sequencing is a robust description of throwing and hitting, but what 'transfer' and 'efficiency' mean mechanically, and whether changing a sequence variable improves anything, are separate questions with much weaker evidence.
objectives: Describe proximal-to-distal sequencing and the mechanical accounts of how distal segments reach high speed.
Explain what energy flow analysis measures and why 'energy transfer' and 'mechanical efficiency' need explicit definitions.
Evaluate a kinetic-chain claim with the seven-question standard, separating between-athlete associations, within-athlete associations and intervention effects.
lessons.executive: The kinetic chain is the most used and least examined idea in baseball development. The description is solid: in skilled throwers and hitters, the pelvis, trunk, arm and implement usually reach peak angular velocity in a proximal-to-distal order. The explanations are more technical than the slogans, and the evidence that changing a sequencing variable improves velocity or bat speed in a given athlete is close to absent. Most studies compare different athletes at one time. Their findings are hypotheses for individuals, not prescriptions, and the same timing change can raise speed and joint loading together.

explore.text: A hypothetical development meeting. A pitcher's report shows that his pelvis and trunk reach peak angular velocity almost simultaneously. A coach proposes drills to 'create separation' so the trunk peaks later, citing studies in which harder throwers had greater separation. A biomechanist asks whether those studies compared pitchers with one another or tracked pitchers who changed. A medical staff member asks what the change would do to arm loading. Each question points to a different kind of evidence.
Write down what you think 'energy transfer from the legs to the arm' means in physical terms. Which measurable quantity would show it?

understand.title: Prerequisite: what a 'kinematic sequence' graph shows

blocks.text: A kinematic sequence graph plots the angular velocity of several segments — typically pelvis, trunk, upper arm or lead arm, and hand or bat — against time. The usual summary is the order and spacing of their peaks and the size of each peak. It is a description of when segments rotate fastest. It does not show forces, energy, or why the peaks occur in that order; those require kinetics.

understand.text: The description: proximal-to-distal sequencing

Across striking and throwing skills, segment motions generally begin and peak in a proximal-to-distal order, with each distal segment reaching a higher peak angular velocity than the one before. Putnam's review stressed that this sequence is not explained by joint moments alone: segment interaction, which changes with segment motion and orientation, is central, and differences in interaction between skills can explain differences in timing ([Putnam, 1993](R-putnam-1993-sequential)). Early three-dimensional work on hitting described the same pattern, with pelvis rotation leading trunk and arm rotation ([Welch et al., 1995](R-welch-1995-hitting)).

understand.caption: A typical proximal-to-distal sequence in pitching (description, not mechanism)

steps.label: Stride and foot contact
steps.text: Lead foot lands; ground reaction forces begin to brake and redirect the body.

steps.label: Pelvis peak
steps.text: Pelvis reaches peak angular velocity about the vertical axis.

steps.label: Trunk peak
steps.text: Upper trunk peaks later and faster; trunk tilt and flexion progress.

steps.label: Elbow extension and humeral internal rotation peaks
steps.text: Arm segments reach peaks of several thousand degrees per second near release.

steps.label: Release
steps.text: Ball leaves the hand; deceleration of the arm and trunk follows.

understand.text: Mechanical accounts of the sequence

Three accounts, compatible with one another, explain how distal segments get fast. First, **interaction torques**: a rapidly rotating proximal segment exerts velocity-dependent moments on the next segment, so the forearm can be accelerated with little elbow muscle torque; induced-acceleration analysis attributes much of elbow extension and wrist flexion velocity near release to these effects ([Hirashima et al., 2008](R-hirashima-2008-kinetic); [Zajac and Gordon, 1989](R-zajac-1989-determining)). Second, **elastic storage**: the trunk and arm are stretched before they shorten, and the shoulder in particular may store and return energy ([Roach et al., 2013](R-roach-2013-elastic)). Third, **energy flow**: joint forces and joint moments move mechanical power between segments, which energy-flow analysis quantifies ([Howenstein et al., 2019](R-howenstein-2019-energy)).
What 'energy transfer' can mean

Energy-flow analysis computes, at each joint, the power delivered by the joint force (joint force power, which moves energy between the two segments without generating any) and by the joint moment acting on each segment (segment torque power). Summing these gives the rate at which each segment gains or loses mechanical energy and from where. In 24 youth pitchers, every energy-flow variable correlated with pitch velocity, most strongly the energy flowing from the trunk into the arm (r = 0.90); energy entering the trunk through joint forces was associated with lower velocity-normalized arm loads, which the authors defined as greater efficiency ([Howenstein et al., 2019](R-howenstein-2019-energy)).

This gives 'transfer' a precise meaning: power crossing a joint in a measured direction. It also shows the limits. The quantity depends on inverse-dynamics outputs, inherits their model and filtering assumptions, and is computed from the same kinematics as velocity, which can inflate correlations. 'Efficiency' in that study is a defined ratio — velocity per unit of arm load — not the everyday sense of 'no wasted motion', and not metabolic efficiency. When someone uses the word, ask for the numerator and the denominator.
Pelvis–trunk relationships

Three different quantities travel under the name 'separation'. The first is an angle: the difference between pelvis and upper-trunk orientation about the vertical (or trunk) axis at an event such as foot contact. The second is a timing interval: the time between peak pelvis and peak trunk angular velocity. The third is a rate: how fast that angle closes. They are related but not interchangeable, and each depends on the segment definitions and projection choices of Lesson 2. A pitcher can show a large separation angle at foot contact and still have nearly simultaneous velocity peaks. Mechanically, a larger angle pre-stretches the trunk's rotators and obliques, and a delay between peaks lets the pelvis decelerate while the trunk accelerates — a pattern consistent with momentum moving up the chain. Whether a given pitcher or hitter benefits from more of any of the three depends on his trunk mobility, his strength and what his arm or hands do next.
Timing, velocity and load

Timing variables tend to move velocity and arm loading together. Across youth to professional pitchers, professionals rotated the upper trunk later in the delivery and had the lowest normalized shoulder torque among skeletally mature groups ([Aguinaldo et al., 2007](R-aguinaldo-2007-effects)). Using mixed models over repeated pitches, Urbin and colleagues found that longer phase times between successive segment peaks were associated with lower kinetics and lower ball speed ([Urbin et al., 2013](R-urbin-2013-associations)). Within individual pitchers, faster pitches coincided with differences in trunk and pelvis rotation and with larger arm kinetics ([Stodden et al., 2005](R-stodden-2005-relationship)).

understand.title: Methodological note: between- and within-athlete relationships

blocks.text: A correlation across athletes asks whether athletes who have more of X also have more of Y. A correlation within athletes asks whether, when a given athlete has more of X, he also has more of Y. The two can differ in size and even in sign. Bigger, stronger pitchers may show greater trunk velocity and greater ball velocity, producing a between-pitcher correlation driven by size and strength; within a pitcher, pitch-to-pitch increases in trunk velocity may relate weakly to velocity. Mixed models with separate within- and between-athlete terms are the standard way to estimate both, and Week 12 returns to them. Neither is an intervention effect: natural variation within a pitcher is not the same as a trained change, which may alter other variables at the same time.

challenge.text: Misconceptions that the evidence does not support

items: **'Energy leaks.'** Mechanical energy is not lost through a gap in a sequence the way water leaks from a pipe. Energy is absorbed by negative joint power, dissipated in tissues or returned to the ground; which of these happens, and whether it costs velocity, has to be computed, not inferred from a video.

**'The arm is just along for the ride.'** Interaction torques make a large contribution to distal speed, but shoulder internal-rotation and elbow moments are large and active. The arm is driven and also drives.

**'There is one correct sequence.'** Skilled throwers and hitters vary in timing, and variability of timing did not decrease with competitive level in a study of pitch-to-pitch variability ([Fleisig et al., 2009](R-fleisig-2009-variability)).

**'More separation is always better.'** Between-athlete associations do not establish a dose–response for an individual, and timing changes that raise speed can also raise load ([Urbin et al., 2013](R-urbin-2013-associations)).

challenge.text: Even the mechanical meaning of the chain is debated. Some accounts emphasize the summation of segment speeds, others the transfer of angular momentum from large to small segments, others energy flow through joint forces. These are different decompositions of the same equations of motion, and each depends on a model; they do not compete as facts so much as answer different questions ([Putnam, 1993](R-putnam-1993-sequential); [Hirashima et al., 2008](R-hirashima-2008-kinetic); [Howenstein et al., 2019](R-howenstein-2019-energy)). The injury side is also uncertain: early trunk rotation has some support as a risk factor, but low power limits most conclusions ([Bullock et al., 2021](R-bullock-2021-baseball)).

The structure of the literature adds its own cautions. Much of the pitching canon comes from one laboratory group and its collaborators, using one family of methods and samples recruited from its network; consistency across those papers is partly consistency of method. Samples of 20 to 40 athletes analysed for dozens of variables invite false positives unless corrections are applied and effects are replicated. Groups split at the extremes of velocity make differences look larger than they are in the middle of the distribution. None of this makes the findings wrong; it makes them hypotheses that deserve independent replication and, eventually, intervention tests.

A later-peaking trunk is stretched more and can receive more energy and momentum from the pelvis; interaction torques then accelerate distal segments.

What are the implications for loading or potential injury-related risk?

apply.text: Pitching and hitting compared

In pitching the distal 'implement' is the hand and ball, with a mass of about 145 g, and the main constraint is the shoulder and elbow's tolerance of the resulting loads. In hitting the implement is a bat of about 0.9 kg, held by both hands, and the swing must be timed to a pitch and adjusted on-line. Sequencing in hitting therefore serves two goals at once: producing bat speed and preserving the ability to change the swing late. A sequence that maximizes bat speed off a tee may compromise adaptability against live pitching, a point tee-based studies cannot test ([Dowling and Fleisig, 2016](R-dowling-2016-kinematic)).

Synthetic illustration of within- versus between-athlete evidence. Five pitchers each throw ten fastballs. Across the five, average trunk peak delay ranges from 20 to 60 ms and correlates strongly with average velocity, because the two pitchers with the longest delays are also the strongest and largest. Within each pitcher, pitch-to-pitch delay varies by about ±8 ms and is nearly uncorrelated with that pitch's velocity. A coach reading only the between-pitcher correlation would prescribe longer delays; the within-pitcher data offer no support for that lever in any of these five pitchers. Real data can show either pattern, which is why both must be estimated.

A practical template for a kinetic-chain observation in a report: state the measurement (e.g. trunk peaks 20 ms after pelvis); state which category of evidence relates it to output (usually between-athlete association); state what is unknown for this athlete; propose a test — a change in a constraint or drill, with velocity, timing and arm kinetics measured before and after, and a retention test weeks later. The plan treats the kinetic-chain idea as a hypothesis about this athlete.

A defensible decision is to pilot the drills with a comparison group, measure velocity and arm kinetics with the same system before and after, include a retention test, and decide in advance what result would stop the program. The cost of not checking is a season of practice time spent on an untested lever, with possible loading costs.

Most evidence is cross-sectional and between athletes; timing changes can move speed and load together; no intervention study shows that changing a sequencing variable raises velocity or bat speed.

lessons.title: Foundations of Motor Control: Redundancy, Variability and Constraints
lessons.summary: The body has far more degrees of freedom than any throw or swing requires, so skilled athletes solve the same task differently on each repetition; variability that leaves the task outcome unchanged is not error, and individual solutions emerge from the interaction of body, environment and task constraints.
objectives: Explain Bernstein's degrees-of-freedom problem and why redundancy is a resource rather than a nuisance.
Distinguish task-relevant from task-irrelevant variability using the uncontrolled-manifold and optimal-feedback-control ideas.
Use Newell's constraints framework to generate competing explanations for an individual movement solution.
lessons.executive: No two pitches from the same pitcher are mechanically identical, and the best pitchers do not show the least variability in every joint. What matters is whether variability shows up in the dimensions that change where and how fast the ball goes. Motor-control theory gives a precise way to ask that question and a reason to expect different athletes to solve the same task with different movements. For a department, the consequence is direct: reducing variability everywhere is not a defensible goal, and a mechanical difference between two athletes is not, by itself, evidence that one of them is wrong.

explore.text: Hypothetical data. A right-handed pitcher's release point varies by about 5 cm from pitch to pitch, while his elbow flexion at release varies by 8° and his trunk tilt by 6°. A second pitcher varies by only 3° and 3° at those joints but by 9 cm at release. Which pitcher is more consistent? The answer depends on which variable the task cares about — and, more subtly, on whether the joint variations of the first pitcher cancel each other out at the hand.

Predict: if you threw at a target fifty times and your elbow angle at release varied by several degrees, would you expect your hand position to vary by the same proportion? What would have to happen at your other joints to keep it steady?

understand.title: Prerequisite: degrees of freedom and redundancy

blocks.text: A task has a goal described by a few variables — for a pitch, release location, release velocity and spin. The body that produces it has many more: the arm alone has seven rotational degrees of freedom from shoulder to wrist, and hundreds of muscles act across them. When many combinations of joint motions produce the same task outcome, the system is **redundant** (also called motor abundance). Redundancy means there is no single correct movement for a goal; there is a family of solutions.

understand.text: Bernstein's problem

Bernstein framed coordination as the mastery of redundant degrees of freedom: converting a body with too many independent parts into a controllable system. He also emphasized that skilled repetition is not reproduction: the performer solves the movement problem again on each attempt, so the details differ while the outcome is preserved ([Bernstein, 1967](R-bernstein-1967-coordination)). Sport biomechanists long treated this between-trial variability as noise to be averaged away; reviews of throwing and other skills argue that even elite performers do not reproduce identical patterns and that some variability is functional ([Bartlett et al., 2007](R-bartlett-2007-is)).
Task-relevant and task-irrelevant variability

The **uncontrolled manifold** method makes the distinction measurable. For a hypothesized task variable — say, hand position at release — the set of joint configurations that leave that variable unchanged forms a manifold in joint space. Between-trial joint variance is split into the component along that manifold, which does not affect the task variable, and the component orthogonal to it, which does. More variance along the manifold than across it indicates that joints co-vary to stabilize the variable ([Scholz and Schöner, 1999](R-scholz-1999-uncontrolled); [Latash et al., 2002](R-latash-2002-motor)).

**Optimal feedback control** offers a reason why. If motor commands are noisy and the controller minimizes a cost that includes task error and effort, the optimal strategy is not to enforce a fixed trajectory but to correct only those deviations that threaten the goal and to let variability accumulate in task-irrelevant dimensions — the minimal intervention principle ([Todorov and Jordan, 2002](R-todorov-2002-optimal)).

understand.text: Feedforward, feedback and internal models

Motor control combines feedforward commands, planned in advance from a prediction of what the body and environment will do, with feedback corrections based on sensory information. Computational accounts propose that the nervous system uses internal models: a forward model predicts the sensory consequences of a motor command, which lets the system estimate the state of the limb despite delayed and noisy sensory signals ([Wolpert et al., 1995](R-wolpert-1995-internal); [Todorov and Jordan, 2002](R-todorov-2002-optimal)). For fast ballistic actions the balance shifts toward feedforward, because sensory delays are long relative to the movement; the quality of the plan, and of the state estimate on which it is based, then determines much of the outcome.

Noise matters in this picture. Motor commands are noisy, and in many tasks the noise grows with the size of the command, so faster and more forceful movements tend to be more variable. A pitcher throwing at maximal intent is operating where command noise is large; part of skill is organizing the redundant joints so that this noise is channelled into dimensions that do not move the ball. This is one reason velocity and command can trade off, and why reducing intent is a common, if crude, way to improve accuracy.
Constraints and individual solutions

Newell proposed that coordination emerges from the interaction of three families of constraints: **organismic** (body size, strength, mobility, tissue properties, perceptual and neural factors), **environmental** (gravity, surfaces, light, temperature) and **task** (the goal, the rules, the implement). Changing any of them changes which coordination patterns are available and which are preferred ([Newell, 1986](R-newell-1986-constraints)). Two pitchers with different humeral torsion, hip mobility and strength face different organismic constraints, so the same goal may be best achieved with different movements.

Dynamical-systems accounts describe coordination with a few collective variables, such as the relative phase between segments, whose stable values (attractors) change with control parameters; when a parameter crosses a threshold, a pattern can lose stability and switch to another ([Kelso, 1995](R-kelso-1995-dynamic)). The strongest experimental support comes from rhythmic tasks such as bimanual finger coordination; applying the vocabulary to a discrete pitch or swing is more interpretive.

understand.title: Methodological note: feedback, feedforward and time

blocks.text: A fastball from release to the plate takes roughly 0.4 s, and the swing itself lasts on the order of 0.15 s. Visual feedback loops take on the order of 0.1–0.2 s to affect movement, so much of a swing must be planned before it begins, and later corrections are limited. A pitch, once the arm is accelerating, is effectively feedforward: arm acceleration lasts only a few hundredths of a second, which is too short for vision-based correction. This is why optimal-feedback-control ideas apply most clearly to the preparation and early phases of these skills, and why Week 8 treats timing and on-line adjustment in hitting separately.

challenge.text: How far the variability argument goes

The functional-variability view holds that healthy, skilled movement shows an optimal amount and structure of variability, and that too little can be as problematic as too much ([Stergiou and Decker, 2011](R-stergiou-2011-human)). The idea is influential but hard to falsify: 'optimal' is rarely specified in advance, much of the supporting evidence comes from gait and clinical populations, and measured variability always includes measurement error that must be separated before it can be interpreted ([Preatoni et al., 2013](R-preatoni-2013-movement)). In baseball, pitch-to-pitch variability of many kinematic and kinetic variables was smaller at higher competitive levels, but timing variability was not ([Fleisig et al., 2009](R-fleisig-2009-variability)) — consistent with reduced noise in skilled pitchers and with persistent variability in coordination timing, and not decisive between theories.

The individual-solutions idea can also be overstated. That many solutions exist does not mean all are equally good for velocity, command or tissue loading. Some solutions are better for a given athlete; some differences are deficiencies. The theory's demand is narrower: a difference has to be shown to matter for this athlete before it is treated as a fault.

How much joint variability is compensated (structure, not size); how much is measurement error; whether release-point variability limits this pitcher's command at all.
Has changing the variable improved performance?
No intervention study shows that reducing joint-angle variability improves command.
Does the improvement transfer to competition?
Unknown; transfer to game command would require competitive outcome measures.
What are the implications for loading or potential injury-related risk?
Unknown; constraining movement variability might concentrate repetitive loading on the same tissue regions, a hypothesis rather than a finding.

apply.text: Applying the ideas to pitching and hitting

For a pitcher, the useful questions are which task variables matter (release location, release direction, velocity, spin axis), how variable each is, and whether joint-level variability is compensated. A pitcher whose trunk tilt varies but whose arm angle relative to the trunk co-varies to keep release height stable is showing coordination, not inconsistency. A pitcher whose release height wanders with his trunk tilt may have a command problem with a mechanical source worth investigating.

For a hitter, the task variables are bat-path timing and bat orientation at contact relative to a pitch that varies. Here variability is partly the point: a hitter must produce different swings for different pitches. Swing-to-swing variability against a tee says little about adaptability against live pitching, and reducing it in tee work is not obviously desirable.

A worked estimate shows why structure matters. Treat the arm from shoulder to hand as a 0.6 m lever. A 2° error in its orientation (0.035 rad) moves the hand by about 0.6 × 0.035 ≈ 2.1 cm. If variations in trunk tilt and in shoulder angle each move the hand by about 2 cm in the same direction and are independent, their effects add in quadrature to about 3 cm; if they are negatively correlated, so that a larger tilt comes with a smaller shoulder angle, the hand moves much less than either variation alone would predict. Release-point variability therefore cannot be read off joint-angle variability without knowing the correlations among joints — the core idea of the uncontrolled manifold.

Newell's framework gives a structured way to generate hypotheses. For a pitcher whose stride is shorter than his peers', list candidate organismic constraints (hip mobility, lead-leg strength), environmental constraints (mound slope, footing) and task constraints (pitch type, intent, the drill), then decide which measurements would distinguish them before prescribing a change.

apply.title: Executive twist: a 'consistency score' in a development dashboard

blocks.text: A proposed dashboard ranks pitchers by a single 'mechanical consistency score' averaged over twenty joint angles. Motor-control theory and the measurement literature both argue against it: it mixes task-relevant and task-irrelevant variability, includes measurement error, and implies that less variability is always better. A defensible alternative reports variability of task outcomes (release point, velocity, location) with measurement error stated, and analyses joint variability only to explain outcome variability that matters.

retain.text: Redundancy means many movements achieve one goal. Variability that leaves the goal unchanged is not error, and optimal-feedback control predicts that skilled performers will allow it. Constraints of body, environment and task shape which solution an athlete uses. The questions for any variability measure are: in which dimension, how much is measurement error, and does it matter for the outcome?
What does the uncontrolled-manifold method partition, and what does a high ratio of along-manifold to across-manifold variance indicate?
Give one organismic, one environmental and one task constraint that could change a hitter's swing.
Why is a single average 'consistency score' over many joints hard to interpret?

takeaways: The body is redundant: many joint combinations produce the same task outcome.
Variability in task-irrelevant dimensions is expected and can be functional; variability that changes the outcome is the concern.
Optimal feedback control predicts minimal intervention: correct only deviations that threaten the goal.
Organismic, environmental and task constraints together shape individual movement solutions.
Measured variability includes measurement error, which must be estimated before variability is interpreted.
