lessons.title: Force Plates, IMUs & EMG
lessons.summary: What ground reaction forces, inertial sensors and electromyography actually measure, how their signals are processed, and why a wearable 'elbow torque' is a model estimate rather than a measured load.
objectives: Derive impulse and centre of pressure from force-plate outputs and identify when each becomes unreliable.
Explain gyroscope drift, accelerometer gravity contamination, sensor fusion and saturation, and apply them to wearable throwing sensors.
Describe the EMG processing chain and state what EMG amplitude can and cannot tell you about muscle force.
lessons.executive: Force plates measure the force between foot and ground directly and well; their limits are installation (a pitching mound must be built around them) and the fact that they measure only the whole-body external force. Inertial sensors measure acceleration and rotation rate on the skin; orientation and position come from integration and fusion, which drift. A wearable elbow sensor does not measure ligament load: it combines arm kinematics with a body model to estimate a net joint moment, and its published comparison to motion capture found the estimate correlated but substantially lower. EMG shows when a muscle is electrically active, not how hard it pulls. None of these numbers is an injury probability.

explore.text: A synthetic right-handed pitcher wears an arm sensor for a bullpen session. His “elbow torque” averages 72 N·m on fastballs this week, against 66 N·m last week. The same week, force plates in the mound show his lead-leg peak vertical force rose from 1.9 to 2.1 body weights. A staff member proposes reducing his throwing volume because “his UCL load is up 9%.” All values are synthetic.
Which of the three numbers in this vignette is measured directly, which is estimated through a model, and which assumption would you test first?

The force-plate value is a direct measurement of the external force, subject to calibration and installation. The sensor's torque is a model output: it combines measured angular velocity and acceleration with assumed arm dimensions and mass properties to estimate a net moment at the elbow — the sum of everything that crosses the joint, not ligament tension. The claim that “UCL load is up 9%” adds two further inferences: that the net moment is borne by the ligament in a fixed proportion, and that a 9% change exceeds the sensor's measurement error. Neither has been shown.

understand.text: Force plates

A force plate measures three orthogonal force components and three moments about its own axes, using strain gauges or piezoelectric crystals at its supports. From these, the point of application of the resultant force on the surface — the centre of pressure (COP) — is computed. For a plate whose origin lies a distance h below its surface, the anteroposterior and mediolateral COP coordinates are obtained from the moments and the vertical force, for example x = (−My − h·Fx)/Fz and y = (Mx − h·Fy)/Fz in one common convention; sign conventions vary by manufacturer and must be checked. Ground reaction force and COP, combined with segment kinematics and inertial properties, are the inputs to inverse dynamics.

Two numbers worth computing. Impulse is the time integral of force, so a lead-leg braking force averaging 0.8 body weight for 0.10 s on a 90 kg pitcher (body weight ≈ 883 N) delivers an anteroposterior impulse of 0.8 × 883 × 0.10 ≈ 71 N·s, enough to change the body's forward momentum by 71 kg·m/s, or its centre-of-mass velocity by about 0.79 m/s. And because COP divides by Fz, when vertical force is small — at initial contact, or as the foot leaves the plate — tiny moment errors produce large COP excursions; laboratories therefore compute COP only above a force threshold.

Force–time curves carry more information than peaks. The rate of force development, the timing of the peak relative to foot contact and ball release, and the impulse in each direction describe how force is produced. In pitching, a mound with embedded plates is required for both legs; in hitting, two plates under the feet in the box allow each leg to be analyzed. Plates must be rigidly mounted, level, and of known natural frequency high enough that impacts do not excite plate vibration; mound installations with turf and clay over the plate change all three.
Inertial measurement units

An inertial measurement unit (IMU) combines a triaxial accelerometer, a triaxial gyroscope and often a magnetometer. The accelerometer measures specific force — linear acceleration minus gravity — in the sensor's own frame; the gyroscope measures angular velocity in that frame. Orientation is obtained by integrating angular velocity, and position by double integration of gravity-corrected acceleration. Both integrations accumulate error, so sensor-fusion algorithms (complementary or Kalman filters) correct orientation using gravity, and sometimes the magnetic field, as references. Camomilla and colleagues' systematic review of in-field sport applications found that most studies were conducted in training rather than competition and highlighted reliability and sensor-to-segment calibration as continuing concerns.

understand.title: Prerequisite: why integration drifts

blocks.text: A gyroscope with an uncorrected bias of 0.5°/s accumulates 30° of orientation error per minute, because the error grows linearly with time. An accelerometer bias of 0.05 m/s², double-integrated over 2 s, gives a position error of ½ × 0.05 × 2² = 0.10 m, and the error grows with the square of time. Short, fast events such as a single throw are less affected than long recordings, which is why throwing sensors reset or re-reference between throws.

understand.text: Three additional IMU problems matter for baseball. Saturation: the throwing arm's angular velocities are among the fastest in sport, and a gyroscope whose range is lower than the peak clips the signal and corrupts every integrated quantity downstream, so check the datasheet range against the task. Sensor-to-segment alignment: the sensor measures its own axes, not the humerus's, so a calibration posture or functional movement is needed to relate them, and a strap that rotates on the arm changes the result. Magnetic disturbance: ferrous structures in stadiums and training facilities distort the magnetometer, so heading estimates indoors can be unreliable.
Wearable elbow-torque sensors

Boddy and colleagues compared a commercial arm sensor with marker-based motion capture during pitching. Arm slot and shoulder rotation correlated with motion-capture values and arm slot averaged about 8° lower; the sensor's “stress” metric correlated with motion-capture elbow varus torque but was about 41 N·m (39%) lower. Several authors were affiliated with a private training company. Camp and colleagues used the same type of sensor on 81 professional pitchers across about 82,000 throws and found within-pitcher relationships between estimated varus torque and arm slot, arm speed and shoulder rotation; that study described associations among sensor outputs and did not validate the sensor.

understand.title: Methodological note: what an inverse-dynamics elbow moment is

blocks.text: Inverse dynamics computes the net joint moment at the elbow as the moment required to produce the observed motion of the forearm–hand segment (and ball), given its mass, centre of mass and moments of inertia and the forces acting on it. The result is a net moment: the resultant of every muscle, ligament, capsule and bony contact force acting across the joint. It cannot partition load among structures. Its accuracy depends on joint-centre location, segment inertial parameters and filtering of the kinematics — the same issues covered in [Marker-Based Motion Capture](#b02-l1).

A single-IMU sensor on the forearm faces a harder problem: it measures one segment's motion and must model the rest, typically assuming segment lengths and masses from body height and mass. Its output is therefore an estimate of an estimate. That it tracks within-pitcher changes in the direction of a laboratory net moment is useful; that its absolute value is the ligament's load is not established and, by construction, cannot be.

understand.text: Electromyography

Electromyography records the electrical activity of muscle fibres. Surface electrodes over a muscle belly pick up a summed signal from many motor units and are susceptible to crosstalk from neighbouring muscles; fine-wire electrodes inserted into a muscle record more selectively, including deep muscles such as the subscapularis, but are invasive and sample a small volume. The European SENIAM project, summarized by Hermens and colleagues from a review of 144 papers, produced recommendations for sensor construction and placement for 27 muscles.

Processing typically involves band-pass filtering to remove movement artifact and high-frequency noise, full-wave rectification, and low-pass filtering to obtain a linear envelope (or computing a moving root-mean-square). Because raw amplitude depends on electrode placement, skin impedance and subcutaneous tissue, amplitudes are normalized — commonly to a maximal voluntary isometric contraction or to the peak within the task — before comparison across muscles or people.

challenge.text: EMG amplitude is not muscle force. The relationship between EMG and force is reasonably monotonic only in isometric conditions for a given muscle; in dynamic movements muscle length and shortening velocity change force for the same activation, the electrode moves relative to the muscle, and the electromechanical delay separates electrical onset from force production. In throwing and swinging, EMG is best read for timing and relative activity patterns, not as a dynamometer.

Force plates have their own boundary conditions. A plate measures only the force at its surface: on a mound, the clay, turf and slope between foot and plate alter both the measured force and its point of application, and a front foot that lands partly off the plate produces a plausible but incomplete curve. Plates also report the whole-body external force, the sum of every segment's mass times acceleration plus weight, and cannot say which segment produced it. Statements such as “the lead leg transferred force into the trunk” require inverse dynamics or energy analysis, with the assumptions those methods carry.

Normalization choices can reverse a conclusion. Normalizing to a maximal isometric contraction can yield values above 100% in ballistic tasks; normalizing to the task's own peak removes information about overall intensity. When two studies disagree about which muscle is “more active” during arm cocking, check first whether they normalized the same way.

Wearable sensors deserve particular scrutiny because they generate large datasets cheaply. A large number of throws does not fix a biased instrument; it estimates the bias precisely. The question for any wearable is the size of its bias and limits of agreement against a reference for the variable you will use, and its within-athlete typical error in the setting where you will use it.

challenge.caption: Applying the standard to: “A wearable sensor's elbow torque tracks UCL load and can guide throwing workload.”
rows: Sensor torque correlates with laboratory net elbow varus moment but reads substantially lower; within-pitcher relationships with arm slot and arm speed have been described.
Kinematics of one segment plus a body model produce an estimated net joint moment.
Boddy et al. 2019 (comparison, company-affiliated); Camp et al. 2017 (association across many throws).
The share of the net moment borne by the ligament; within-pitcher typical error in games; tissue capacity, which is not measured at all.
Has changing the variable improved performance?
No evidence was reviewed that sensor-guided workload decisions improve performance.
Does the improvement transfer to competition?
Not applicable to performance; the claim concerns health monitoring.
What are the implications for loading or potential injury-related risk?
A net joint moment is a mechanical load estimate, not a ligament load and not an injury probability; injury decisions belong to medical staff.

items: **(1) Biomechanical measurement:** The sensor measures arm kinematics directly and estimates net moment through a model with known bias.
**(2) Mechanics → mechanical output:** Within-pitcher associations between estimated torque and arm speed are reported.
**(3) Mechanics → competitive outcome:** No link from sensor torque to competitive outcome is reviewed here.
**(4) Demonstrated intervention effect:** No trial shows that managing throwing by sensor torque changes outcomes.
**(5) Retention and transfer:** Not studied for retention or transfer.

apply.text: Return to the vignette. The 6 N·m increase in estimated torque coincided with a rise in lead-leg force, which suggests the pitcher threw harder; higher arm speed is associated with higher estimated torque in Camp et al. Before any decision, ask for the sensor's within-pitcher typical error from repeated sessions, confirm the strap position and sensor firmware were unchanged, and check velocity. The appropriate output to the medical and performance staff is a description — “estimated net elbow moment increased by an amount near the measurement error while velocity rose” — not “UCL load is up 9%.” Workload decisions remain clinical and multidisciplinary.

For hitters, force plates under each foot and IMUs on the bat and lead forearm are the practical field kit. Bat-mounted sensors measure the bat's own motion, a rigid body with known geometry, which is a friendlier problem than estimating joint angles from skin-mounted sensors. Their bat-speed definitions differ from tracking definitions, so values from a sensor and from stadium tracking should not be compared directly.

State in writing that the sensor estimates a net joint moment and does not measure ligament load or injury risk.

lessons.title: Video, Ball Tracking & Bat Tracking
lessons.summary: How frame rate, exposure and camera geometry limit what video can resolve, what stadium ball- and bat-tracking metrics are defined to mean, and why tracking outputs are not a biomechanical assessment.
objectives: Calculate the temporal and angular resolution of video for fast pitching and hitting events.
Quantify perspective error in 2D analysis and explain when 3D reconstruction is required.
State the published definitions of tracking-derived bat metrics and distinguish them from body kinematics, including synchronization requirements for integrating systems.
lessons.executive: Video is limited by time and geometry. At 240 frames per second, a shoulder rotating at 7,000°/s moves about 29° between frames, and a millisecond-scale bat–ball contact usually falls between frames entirely. A single camera sees angles projected onto its image plane, so a 45° segment can read 49° or more when the plane of motion is rotated. Stadium tracking systems such as Hawk-Eye produce precise outputs about the ball and the bat — bat speed at the sweet spot, swing length, attack angle — but these describe the implement, not the body that produced it. They are mechanical outputs; they are not a biomechanical assessment.

explore.text: A hitting coach films a synthetic hitter at 240 frames per second from the open side and reports that the bat “was level through contact” and that the hitter's lead elbow “extended at 30° before contact.” The stadium bat-tracking output for the same swing reports an attack angle of 14°. Values are synthetic.
Before reading on: at 240 frames per second, how far does a bat sweet spot moving at 32 m/s travel between consecutive frames? Could the coach have seen contact?

The interval between frames is 1/240 s ≈ 4.17 ms. The sweet spot travels 32 × 0.00417 ≈ 0.13 m — about five inches — between frames. If bat–ball contact lasts on the order of a millisecond (take 1 ms as a working value), the chance that any given frame falls within contact is about 1/4.17 ≈ 0.24. Most 240 Hz swings have no frame at contact; “through contact” is an interpolation. And an elbow angle read from one camera depends on the camera's position, as the next section shows.

understand.text: Temporal resolution

Sampling theory requires a sampling rate of at least twice the highest frequency present in the signal to avoid aliasing; in practice biomechanists sample several times higher than the frequencies of interest so that peaks and event timing are resolved. Each frame is also an exposure of finite duration: a short shutter limits motion blur, at the cost of light.

understand.caption: What different frame rates resolve for fast baseball events (working values)
headers: Expected frames during a 1 ms contact
understand.note: Arithmetic on working values chosen for illustration: 7,000°/s as an order-of-magnitude shoulder internal-rotation peak, 32 m/s as a bat sweet-spot speed and 1 ms as a contact duration. Not measured data.

understand.text: Two consequences follow for peaks and timing. A sampled peak is the largest sample, not the largest value; with 29° between samples, the true peak can lie anywhere between frames, and smoothing reduces it further. Event timing — foot contact, maximum external rotation, release, contact — is uncertain by up to half a frame interval either side, about ±2 ms at 240 Hz. Sequencing claims built on differences of a few milliseconds between segment peaks need either higher sampling or explicit uncertainty.

Exposure is the second constraint. A frame exposed for 1/1,000 s while a ball travels at 40 m/s smears the ball over 40 mm, more than half its diameter; the hand at release, moving at a comparable speed, blurs similarly. Pose models and human coders then locate a blurred hand or bat less precisely. Shortening exposure to 1/4,000 s reduces the smear to 10 mm but needs four times the light, which is why high-speed capture outdoors at night or in a dim cage often trades frame rate or exposure for image quality.

Interpolating between frames recovers some lost information when the movement is smooth, but not when it is not. A smooth trunk rotation can be fitted between samples well; the instant of bat–ball contact, a discontinuity in the ball's velocity, cannot be reconstructed from frames on either side unless you model the collision itself. Tracking systems therefore estimate contact from trajectories of ball and bat before and after the event rather than from an image of it.
Geometry: 2D versus 3D

A single camera projects the world onto its image plane. Consider a segment inclined 45° above horizontal in a plane rotated 30° away from the camera's image plane about the vertical axis. Its horizontal extent appears shortened by cos 30° ≈ 0.866, its vertical extent is unchanged, and its apparent inclination becomes atan(tan 45° / cos 30°) = atan(1.155) ≈ 49.1°. Rotate the plane 60° away and the same segment appears at atan(2) ≈ 63.4°. Lens distortion and the athlete moving toward or away from the camera add further error.

understand.title: Prerequisite: when 2D analysis is legitimate

blocks.text: Two-dimensional analysis is valid only for motion that stays in a plane parallel to the image plane, with the camera far enough away and perpendicular to that plane, and with the scale known in that plane. Pitching and hitting are three-dimensional rotations: trunk rotation, shoulder rotation and bat path are all out of any single plane. Two-dimensional video is excellent for timing qualitative events, counting, and communication with athletes; it is not a measurement of joint angles in throwing or swinging. Three-dimensional reconstruction requires at least two calibrated, synchronized views of each point of interest.

understand.text: Stadium ball and bat tracking

Major League Baseball's Statcast system has used Hawk-Eye optical tracking since 2020, with twelve cameras around each park for pitch, batted-ball and player tracking and a pose-tracking capability that follows players' body positions. MLB's 2020 description listed 100 frames per second for the cameras dedicated to pitch tracking; later press coverage of bat tracking described higher frame rates that we could not confirm from a primary MLB source.

Statcast's bat-tracking glossary defines bat speed as the speed of the bat's sweet spot at the point of contact, or where contact would have occurred on a miss; a player's average is computed from the faster portion of his swings. Swing length is the total distance in feet travelled by the head of the bat in three dimensions from the start of tracking until impact. Attack angle is the vertical direction in which the sweet spot is travelling at contact. These are defined properties of the bat's motion, computed from tracked bat positions.

Ball-tracking release measurements — release height, side, extension, velocity, spin rate and axis — are similarly properties of the ball at or after release, reconstructed from the trajectory. Extension, for instance, is a ball position, not a measure of stride length or trunk posture, though both influence it.

understand.title: Methodological note: synchronizing and integrating systems

blocks.text: Combining instruments — force plates at 1,000 Hz, marker cameras at 240 Hz, a radar or tracking system, EMG at 2,000 Hz — requires a common time base. Hardware synchronization uses a shared trigger or clock; software synchronization aligns timestamps or detected events after the fact. Data at different rates are resampled to a common rate, and filters must be matched before signals are combined in inverse dynamics.

The size of a synchronization error is easy to compute. An offset of one 240 Hz frame (4.17 ms) between force and motion data, when the bat is moving at 32 m/s, places the bat about 0.13 m from where it was when the force was recorded; at foot contact, it shifts the onset of ground force relative to the stride by the same interval. Pairing a tracking system's contact time with a markerless system's swing frames inherits both systems' clocks and both systems' event definitions. Every integrated report should state how synchronization was achieved and verified.

Tracking outputs and body kinematics also come with different definitions of the same event. “Contact” in bat tracking is a modelled bat–ball intersection; “ball release” in markerless pitching is often a detected instant from hand–ball separation in video. Studies that combine them — for example, Hoechstetter et al.'s analysis pairing in-game markerless kinematics with ball-tracking data — must align these events; check how.

challenge.text: The central error in applied practice is treating tracking outputs as biomechanics. Bat speed, attack angle and swing length tell you what the bat did. They do not tell you how the body produced it, what the joints experienced, or which of many movement solutions the hitter used. Two hitters with identical bat speed can differ greatly in pelvis–trunk timing, and one hitter can produce the same attack angle with different body postures in different pitch locations. Release metrics similarly describe the ball, not the arm.

Definitions also embed choices that affect interpretation. Average bat speed computed from the faster swings excludes checked and defensive swings, which is sensible for estimating capacity but means the average is not a mean of all swings. Attack angle is read at the contact point, and the bat's arc through the zone means that contact at a different pitch height or depth can change the angle, so a change in attack angle can reflect pitch location rather than a change in swing. Changes in the tracking system or its algorithms can shift league-wide distributions. Statcast's definitions are published, but their measurement error for an individual swing is not, to our knowledge, documented in a peer-reviewed validation.

Body pose tracked by a stadium system raises the same questions as any markerless system, plus two of its own. The cameras were placed for ball tracking and broadcast-scale coverage, not for joint-level biomechanics, so occlusion and viewing angles for the throwing arm or the hitter's hands may be unfavourable. And the pose outputs available to clubs may be produced at a lower rate, or with a different skeletal model, from the ball tracking. Aguinaldo and colleagues' comparison is the only peer-reviewed evaluation we found of an in-stadium Hawk-Eye installation for pitching biomechanics; it found joint position errors of the order of 5–6 cm and the weakest agreement for shoulder rotation.

challenge.caption: Applying the standard to: “Raising a hitter's tracked bat speed by 2 mph will improve his results.”
rows: Bat speed is a tracked property of the bat at contact; harder-hit balls require faster bats, other things being equal.
Momentum transfer at collision: higher bat speed at the sweet spot raises potential exit velocity, if contact quality is maintained.
Collision physics supports the mechanical relationship; tracking data describe distributions of bat speed among hitters.
Whether a training-induced increase preserves contact rate, timing and pitch selection; the individual-swing measurement error of the tracking system.
Has changing the variable improved performance?
Not established here: whether interventions that raise bat speed improve competitive results for a given hitter.
Does the improvement transfer to competition?
Unknown without a game-based evaluation over sufficient plate appearances.
What are the implications for loading or potential injury-related risk?
Faster swings and heavier training implements may change loading; no inference about injury is supported by tracking data.

items: **(1) Biomechanical measurement:** Bat speed is a well-defined tracking output; its per-swing error is not documented in the peer-reviewed literature we reviewed.
**(2) Mechanics → mechanical output:** Higher bat speed raises potential exit velocity through collision physics (Week 7 develops this).
**(3) Mechanics → competitive outcome:** Relationships between bat speed and outcomes depend on contact, timing and decisions; they are not established for individuals by tracking alone.
**(4) Demonstrated intervention effect:** Intervention evidence for bat-speed training and its effect on game results is not reviewed this week.
**(5) Retention and transfer:** Retention and transfer require repeated in-game measurement over time.

apply.text: Rewrite the coach's report. “Level through contact” cannot be observed at 240 Hz from one side and conflicts with a tracked attack angle of 14°; the tracked value is the better estimate of bat direction at contact, subject to the system's unknown per-swing error, and it should be read against the pitch's location. The elbow angle should be described as a 2D projected angle from a stated camera position, used for qualitative comparison between swings filmed identically, not as a joint measurement.

For a pitcher, combine instruments by question. Release consistency across a season: ball-tracking release data. Arm path timing within the delivery: high-speed video at 480 Hz or more from fixed, documented positions, or markerless capture. Joint angles and moments: 3D capture with synchronized force plates in a laboratory. A report that mixes these should label each number with its instrument.

blocks.text: A department can buy six 240 Hz cameras for every minor-league affiliate or two 1,000 Hz cameras for one facility. The right answer depends on the decision. For event timing and qualitative review at scale, consistent 240 Hz views across affiliates may be more valuable; for questions about contact, release or rapid arm rotation, only higher rates resolve the event. Specify the event you need to resolve, compute the frame interval required, and buy to that requirement.

retain.text: Frame rate sets what can be seen in time; camera geometry sets what can be seen in space; tracking systems describe the ball and bat precisely by published definitions but do not describe the body. Integrating instruments requires a common clock and shared event definitions.
How many frames, on average, fall within a 1 ms contact at 480 Hz?
Why can a 2D elbow angle change when nothing about the elbow changed?
State the Statcast definition of attack angle and one reason it can change without a change in the hitter's swing.

Two-dimensional angles are projections; out-of-plane rotation produces systematic error.
Bat speed, swing length and attack angle have published Statcast definitions about the bat, not the body.
Integrating systems requires synchronization and shared event definitions, which reports should state.

lessons.title: Reliability, Validity & Measurement Error
lessons.summary: The statistics that decide whether a biomechanical number can support a decision: typical error, ICC forms, Bland–Altman limits of agreement, minimal detectable change, and within-athlete variability, worked through with real arithmetic.
objectives: Distinguish accuracy from precision and reliability from validity, and match each to the statistic that estimates it.
Calculate typical error, ICC, limits of agreement and MDC95 from trial or session data.
Judge whether an observed change in an athlete exceeds measurement error and biological variability for a specific decision.
lessons.executive: Every biomechanical number has an error band, and decisions about individual athletes live inside it. Typical error is the standard deviation of an athlete's repeated measurements; from it, the minimal detectable change at 95% confidence is about 2.77 times the typical error. ICC is a ratio of between-athlete to total variance, so it is high in heterogeneous samples and says little about whether one athlete changed. Bland–Altman bias and limits of agreement tell you whether two systems can be swapped; correlation cannot. Before acting on a mechanical change, require that it exceed the MDC from the same system, and that the comparison not cross systems.

explore.text: A synthetic pitcher's peak shoulder external rotation is 177° (mean of 10 fastballs) in a laboratory session in January. After a six-week mobility and drill block he measures 171° in the same laboratory. A second analyst points out that his March in-game markerless value is 166°. The development staff want to know whether the drill block reduced his layback, and by how much.
Write down what you would need to know to answer — about the instrument, about the athlete's normal variation, and about the comparison — before you calculate anything.

You need four things: the laboratory's session-to-session typical error for this variable in pitchers like him; his own trial-to-trial variability within a session; the bias between the laboratory and the in-game system; and whether the change matters for any decision. This lesson builds each from data.

understand.text: Four distinctions

understand.title: Prerequisite: variance, standard deviation and why errors add in quadrature

blocks.text: The standard deviation is the square root of the variance, the average squared deviation from the mean. When two independent sources of error combine, their variances add, not their standard deviations: a change score built from two measurements, each with error SD σ, has variance 2σ² and SD √2·σ. Likewise, a measured value that contains independent biological variation (SD 2.5°) and instrument error (SD 1.5°) has total SD √(2.5² + 1.5²) ≈ 2.9°, not 4.0°. Averaging k independent trials divides the variance by k and the SD by √k. These three rules generate every formula in this lesson.

The 1.96 multiplier comes from the normal distribution: 95% of values from a normal distribution lie within 1.96 standard deviations of its mean. Using it assumes errors are roughly normal and unrelated to the size of the measurement; when that fails, a transformation or a nonparametric interval is needed.

understand.text: **Accuracy** is closeness to the true value; **precision** is closeness of repeated measurements to one another. **Validity** asks whether an instrument measures what it claims, usually assessed against a reference; **reliability** asks whether it gives consistent results on repetition. Hopkins identifies three components of reliability: within-subject random variation (the typical error), systematic change in the mean between trials, and the retest correlation. Atkinson and Nevill emphasize that the choice of statistic should follow from how the measurement will be used, and that relative indices such as correlations must be complemented by absolute indices in the units of measurement.

understand.caption: Accuracy and precision are independent
cells: Scattered and offset: useless for individuals and groups.
Tight but offset: good for tracking change within the system; wrong absolute values (typical of a system-specific bias).
Scattered around the truth: group means are fine, individual values are not.
Tight and centred: the goal, rarely achieved for long-axis joint rotations.
understand.note: A markerless system with a constant offset from the marker system sits in the lower-right cell for within-system monitoring and the upper-left problem disappears only if you never mix systems.

understand.text: Typical error and the minimal detectable change

In a two-session test–retest design, the typical error (TE) equals the standard deviation of the difference scores divided by √2, because each difference contains the error of two measurements. To decide whether an individual's change exceeds error at 95% confidence, the change score's error (√2 × TE) is multiplied by 1.96, giving the minimal detectable change MDC95 = 1.96 × √2 × TE ≈ 2.77 × TE. Weir derives the same quantity from the standard error of measurement.

understand.caption: Synthetic test–retest data: peak shoulder external rotation (°), laboratory marker-based system, eight pitchers, sessions one week apart; each value is a mean of ten fastballs
understand.note: Synthetic data constructed for teaching. Mean difference 1.375°; SD of differences 2.615°.

understand.text: Work it through. The mean difference is 1.38°, a small systematic shift (perhaps a learning or warm-up effect). The standard deviation of the eight differences is 2.62°. Typical error = 2.62 / √2 = 1.85°. MDC95 = 1.96 × √2 × 1.85 = 5.13°. A single pitcher's session-to-session change must exceed about 5° before you can be 95% confident it is not error. Note what this typical error contains: because each session value is a session mean, it includes day-to-day biological variation as well as instrument error, which is appropriate when the decision concerns change across days.
ICC: what it measures, and its forms

The intraclass correlation coefficient expresses reliability as the proportion of total variance that lies between subjects. Koo and Li describe ten forms defined by three choices — the model (one-way random, two-way random, two-way mixed), the type (single measurement or mean of k measurements) and the definition (absolute agreement or consistency) — and recommend reporting all three with confidence intervals, interpreting the lower confidence bound: below 0.5 poor, 0.5–0.75 moderate, 0.75–0.9 good, above 0.9 excellent.

For the eight pitchers above, a two-way ANOVA gives a between-pitcher mean square of 98.71, a between-session mean square of 7.56 and an error mean square of 3.42. ICC(3,1), consistency, single measure = (98.71 − 3.42) / (98.71 + 3.42) = 0.93. ICC(2,1), absolute agreement, single measure = (98.71 − 3.42) / (98.71 + 3.42 + 2 × (7.56 − 3.42) / 8) = 0.92; the small systematic shift lowers absolute agreement slightly. The square root of the error mean square, 1.85°, equals the typical error computed from the differences.

understand.title: Methodological note: why ICC can mislead about individuals

blocks.text: ICC ≈ σ²between / (σ²between + σ²error). Hold the error constant at TE = 1.85° (σ²error = 3.42). In a heterogeneous sample whose true between-pitcher SD is 6.7°, ICC ≈ 44.9 / (44.9 + 3.42) ≈ 0.93. In a homogeneous group — pitchers selected for similar layback, SD 2.5° — ICC ≈ 6.25 / (6.25 + 3.42) ≈ 0.65. The instrument is identical and the MDC is identical; only the sample changed. ICC answers “can this measure rank athletes in this population?” The typical error and MDC answer “can it detect change in one athlete?” Report both.

understand.text: Agreement between systems: Bland–Altman

Bland and Altman argued that correlation is inappropriate for comparing two measurement methods, because two methods can be highly correlated while disagreeing substantially. Their method plots each pair's difference against its mean and reports the mean difference (bias) and the 95% limits of agreement, bias ± 1.96 × SD of the differences, with a check for whether the difference changes with magnitude.

understand.caption: Synthetic paired data: the same pitches captured simultaneously by a laboratory marker-based system and a field markerless system, peak shoulder external rotation (°)
understand.note: Synthetic data. Bias −7.88°; SD of differences 2.17°; limits of agreement −12.12° to −3.63°.

understand.text: The field system reads 7.9° lower on average. The limits of agreement are −7.88 ± 1.96 × 2.17, from −12.1° to −3.6°: for an individual pitch, the field value is expected to be between about 4° and 12° below the laboratory value. Correlation between the two columns is high (the rankings agree), which is exactly the situation Bland and Altman warned about. Looking at the last column, the largest differences occur at the largest means, a hint of proportional bias that a larger sample should test.

Bland and Altman also stressed two refinements that validation reports often omit. The bias is an estimate with its own confidence interval, which with eight pairs is wide; and when the differences grow with the magnitude of the measurement — proportional bias — a single pair of limits misrepresents agreement at both ends of the range, so differences should be modelled against the mean or analyzed on a transformed scale.

challenge.text: Within-athlete variability is not noise to be averaged away; it is part of the athlete. The same synthetic pitcher's ten fastballs in one session produce peak external rotation values of 176, 179, 174, 178, 181, 175, 177, 180, 173 and 177°: mean 177.0°, SD 2.58°. The standard error of the ten-pitch mean is 2.58 / √10 = 0.82°, so the session mean is estimated precisely, but any single pitch can sit 4–5° from it. Comparing one pitch before with one pitch after a drill block conflates pitch-to-pitch variation with change. Averaging trials reduces the random component of error by √k only if trial errors are independent; it does not touch bias, and it does not remove real day-to-day variation.

Whether a value that exceeds the MDC is meaningful remains a separate question. MDC addresses statistical detectability; it says nothing about whether the change matters. Atkinson and Nevill argue that acceptable measurement error should be judged against an analytical goal set by the intended use; sports-science practice often expresses that goal as a smallest worthwhile change tied to performance. For most biomechanical variables, however, no such anchor exists, because the variable's relationship to performance or health for an individual is not established. Lerch and colleagues' finding that within-pitcher variability was similar across in-game and laboratory settings for most variables, alongside large differences in means, shows why both random and systematic components must be estimated in the setting of use.
Measurement uncertainty and fitness for purpose

Measurement uncertainty is the honest statement of the range within which the true value plausibly lies, combining every known component: random error, residual bias after any correction, the uncertainty of the correction itself, and biological variability if the target is the athlete's usual value rather than one pitch. For the opening pitcher, a laboratory session mean of 171° carries a within-session standard error of about 0.8° from pitch-to-pitch variation, but a day-to-day typical error of 1.85° if the question is his usual layback this month. Which uncertainty applies depends on the question.

items: **Name the decision.** What will you do differently depending on the number, and what size of change would alter that action?
**Match the error to the decision.** Use the typical error from the same system, setting, athlete population and variable; require MDC smaller than the change that matters.
**Keep comparisons within one system and version,** or apply a correction only with the uncertainty of the correction stated.
**Decide how many trials to average,** given that averaging reduces random error and pitch-to-pitch variability but not bias or genuine day-to-day change.
**Re-estimate error periodically,** because hardware, software, installation and athletes change.

challenge.text: Atkinson and Nevill frame this as setting an analytical goal before collecting reliability data: an instrument is not reliable or unreliable in the abstract, but adequate or inadequate for detecting a change of a specified size in a specified use. Weir makes the same point in practice by deriving the minimal difference from the SEM rather than relying on an ICC threshold.

challenge.caption: Applying the standard to: “A 6° decrease in peak shoulder external rotation after a drill block shows the drill worked.”
rows: Laboratory session mean fell from 177° to 171°, a change of 6°.
The drill changed arm-cocking mechanics, reducing layback.
The change exceeds this laboratory's MDC95 of 5.1°, so it is probably not measurement error alone.
Whether reduced layback was the goal; whether it reflects the drill, fatigue, mobility or season timing; whether it persists. No control condition.
Has changing the variable improved performance?
Not shown: no velocity, command or other performance change is reported, and a mechanical change is not an improvement by itself.
Does the improvement transfer to competition?
Not tested: retention after the drill ends, and in-game values from the same system.
What are the implications for loading or potential injury-related risk?
Less external rotation is not, by itself, lower injury risk; any loading interpretation requires kinetics and clinical input.

items: **(1) Biomechanical measurement:** A 6° change exceeds the same-system MDC95 (5.1°); comparing with the in-game value would cross systems with a −7.9° bias.
**(2) Mechanics → mechanical output:** Whether layback is related to velocity for this pitcher is not established by this measurement.
**(3) Mechanics → competitive outcome:** No competitive outcome is involved.
**(4) Demonstrated intervention effect:** A single pre–post change without a control cannot attribute cause to the drill.
**(5) Retention and transfer:** Retention and transfer require a delayed retest and in-game data from one system.

apply.text: Answer the opening question. Laboratory to laboratory, 177° to 171° is a 6° change, just beyond the MDC95 of 5.1°: probably real, modestly so, with a single-pitcher pre–post design that cannot attribute it to the drill. The March in-game value of 166° cannot be compared with either laboratory value without correcting for the system bias; using the synthetic agreement data, 166° in the field corresponds to a laboratory value of roughly 166 + 7.9 ≈ 174°, with an individual-level uncertainty spanning the limits of agreement (about 170°–178°). The in-game number offers no evidence of a further decrease. The right report says: “Probable decrease of about 6° in the laboratory; cause not established; in-game value not comparable without correction; retest in the laboratory in four weeks and establish an in-game baseline.”

For hitters, the same arithmetic applies to tracked bat speed. If a hitter's game-to-game typical error in average bat speed is, say, 0.9 mph (a synthetic value), the MDC95 is 2.5 mph; a 1.5 mph increase after an off-season program is not yet distinguishable from variation. Measure the typical error from your own data before you set targets.

blocks.text: An analyst proposes coloring a pitcher's dashboard tile red whenever a mechanical variable changes by more than 5% from his baseline. For a variable near 175°, 5% is 8.8°, larger than the MDC; for a variable near 20°, 5% is 1°, far smaller than any plausible error. Percent thresholds applied uniformly guarantee false alarms on some variables and missed changes on others. Set each variable's threshold from its own typical error in the system and setting where it is collected, and document it beside the tile.

retain.text: Accuracy is about bias, precision about random error; validity needs a reference, reliability needs repetition. Typical error and MDC answer individual questions; ICC answers ranking questions in a particular sample; Bland–Altman answers interchangeability. A change matters only if it exceeds error in the same system and connects to a decision.
Compute MDC95 for a typical error of 2.4°.
Why can a measure have an ICC of 0.95 and still be unable to detect a 4° change in one athlete?
What two numbers from a Bland–Altman analysis would you need before comparing an athlete's laboratory and in-game values?

takeaways: Typical error = SD of test–retest differences / √2; MDC95 = 1.96 × √2 × TE ≈ 2.77 × TE.
ICC depends on sample heterogeneity and must be reported with its model, type, definition and confidence interval.
Bland–Altman bias and limits of agreement, not correlation, decide whether two systems are interchangeable.
Within-athlete variability is real; averaging trials shrinks random error but not bias.
A statistically detectable change is not automatically a meaningful or beneficial one.

check.prompt: Test–retest differences for a variable have a standard deviation of 3.4°. What is the typical error?
check.explanation: Each difference contains the error of two measurements, so its variance is twice the single-measurement error variance; dividing the SD by √2 recovers the typical error of one measurement.

check.prompt: Two systems' peak elbow flexion values correlate at r = 0.96 across 40 pitchers. What can you conclude about interchangeability?

options.text: The systems are interchangeable because the correlation is very high.
Nothing yet: correlation can be high despite a large bias or wide limits of agreement.
The systems disagree, because r is below 1.
The newer system is valid.

check.explanation: Bland and Altman showed that correlation measures association, not agreement. One system could read 10° higher on every pitch and still correlate almost perfectly. Interchangeability requires bias and limits of agreement in the units of measurement.

optionFeedback.a: High correlation is compatible with a large constant or proportional bias.
optionFeedback.c: Some disagreement is expected; the question is whether bias and limits are small enough for the decision.
optionFeedback.d: Agreement with another imperfect system does not establish validity.

check.prompt: The same instrument and protocol produce ICC = 0.93 in one sample and ICC = 0.65 in another. The typical error is identical. The most likely explanation is…

options.text: the second sample's athletes are more homogeneous
the second sample was measured less accurately
the ICC form differed between samples
the second sample was larger

check.explanation: ICC is the ratio of between-subject variance to total variance. With the same error variance, a more homogeneous sample has less between-subject variance and therefore a lower ICC, though the ability to detect change in an individual (MDC) is unchanged.

optionFeedback.b: The typical error is identical, so measurement precision did not change.
optionFeedback.c: Different forms can change ICC, but the stem holds the protocol constant; heterogeneity explains this pattern directly.
optionFeedback.d: Sample size changes the precision of the ICC estimate, not its expected value.

glossary.definition: A sphere coated to reflect infrared light back toward its source, whose 3D position an optical system reconstructs by triangulation from two or more cameras.
Motion of skin-mounted markers relative to the underlying bone caused by skin sliding, muscle deformation and inertial effects; the dominant error in marker-based bone kinematics.
A joint centre estimated from the relative motion of two segments, for example by fitting the centre of the spheres traced by markers about a ball joint.
A joint centre located from palpated anatomical landmarks using regression equations derived from reference samples.
A method for choosing a low-pass filter cut-off by examining the RMS difference between raw and filtered signals across cut-off frequencies.
Detection of body keypoints in images by a trained neural network; in multi-camera systems the 2D detections are combined into a 3D skeletal model.
A point a pose-estimation model is trained to locate in an image, such as a visual estimate of the elbow; not necessarily an anatomical joint centre.

A smoothed amplitude profile of an EMG signal obtained by full-wave rectification followed by low-pass filtering.
Expressing EMG amplitude relative to a reference, such as a maximal voluntary isometric contraction or the task peak, so that amplitudes can be compared.
Half the sampling rate; signal content above it cannot be represented and aliases to lower frequencies.

The standard deviation of an individual's repeated measurements; from two trials, the SD of difference scores divided by √2.

The proportion of total variance due to differences between subjects; its value depends on the model, type, definition and the sample's heterogeneity.

exercise.title: The Measurement Science Laboratory

intro.text: Two fictional systems measure the same synthetic right-handed pitcher: a laboratory marker-based system and a field markerless system. You control four quantities — the field system's systematic bias, each system's random error, the pitcher's within-athlete (pitch-to-pitch and day-to-day) variability, and a true change in his mechanics between two test occasions. The laboratory then generates trials and shows synchronized shoulder and trunk traces from both systems, joint-angle comparisons pitch by pitch, a Bland–Altman plot with bias and limits of agreement, typical error, ICC and MDC95.

items: Start with zero true change and find the smallest bias at which a lab-to-field comparison would wrongly report a real change.
Increase random error until the MDC95 exceeds the true change you set; note how ICC behaves when you change between-athlete spread instead.
Raise within-athlete variability while holding instrument error constant; compare single-pitch and ten-pitch-mean decisions.
For each scenario, record your judgement — real change, not distinguishable from error, or not comparable — before revealing the true value.

intro.text: Notice which statistics move together and which do not. In particular, watch whether waveform similarity stays high while bias grows, and whether ICC rises when you widen the sample rather than improve the instrument.

tasks.prompt: A system’s typical error for single trials is **2.0°**. Compute the 95% minimal detectable change for single trials.
Same system, but you compare the **means of 9 trials** in each session. What is the MDC95 now (assuming independent trials)?
tasks.explain: Averaging n independent trials divides the error by √n: 5.54 ÷ 3 ≈ 1.85°. Trials from one session are rarely fully independent, so treat this as a best case.

tasks.prompt: System B reads exactly 6° higher than System A on every trial. What happens to the correlation between the two systems?

options.text: Nothing — a constant offset leaves the correlation unchanged
It falls in proportion to the bias
It becomes negative

tasks.explain: Correlation measures association, not agreement. That is why validation studies report bias and limits of agreement.

tasks.prompt: Press **Reset settings** (true change 4°, n = 10). Using the **Is the change real?** tab, does **System A**’s observed change exceed its MDC for 10-trial means?

options.text: Yes
No

tasks.explain: The engine computes the verdict from the same simulation you are looking at.

tasks.prompt: Same settings. Does **System B**’s observed change exceed **its** MDC?

options.text: Yes
No

tasks.explain: Same athlete, same true change — but the noisier system cannot distinguish it from error. Whether a change is “real” depends on the measurement as much as on the athlete.

tasks.prompt: Raise the between-athlete spread from 8° to 15°. The ICC for both systems rises. What changed?

options.text: Both systems became more precise
The squad became more heterogeneous; the measurement error did not change
The bias was removed

tasks.explain: ICC is a ratio of between-athlete variance to total variance. Typical error and MDC, in the measurement’s own units, are the athlete-level answer.

debrief.text: The laboratory shows three things. First, a constant bias is invisible within one system and decisive across systems: if baseline and follow-up come from different instruments, a bias of a few degrees manufactures or hides change. Second, the minimal detectable change depends on random error and within-athlete variability in the setting of use, not on the ICC, which also responds to how different the athletes are from one another. Third, averaging pitches shrinks random variation by roughly the square root of the number of trials, but it never removes bias.

It does not show which system is closer to the truth: both are simulated against a known true value that real data never provide. It does not tell you whether a real change in layback matters for performance or health — that requires the evidence tiers you applied in each lesson. And its error model is simpler than reality: real errors can be proportional to magnitude, differ between pitch types, and change when software is updated.

assumptions: All athlete data are synthetic and generated from a known true value; no real athlete, system or club is represented.
Random errors are normally distributed, independent between trials and constant across the measurement range unless proportional bias is switched on.
System bias is constant for a given setting; within-athlete variability is shared by both systems because they measure the same pitches.
MDC95 is computed as 1.96 × √2 × typical error; limits of agreement as bias ± 1.96 × SD of paired differences; ICC as a two-way model, single measurement.
The fictional systems are not models of any commercial product.

case.title: Validated Against What? Critiquing a Markerless Pitching Study
case.fiction: The study summarized is real and cited from verified records. The club, its people, the vendor's deck and all numbers in the exhibit are fictional or synthetic.

body.text: This case asks you to critique a real, peer-reviewed validation study. The study is summarized in our own words from its published abstract and verified bibliographic records; the decision context — a development department at a fictional professional club, its people and its data — is invented.
The decision

Dana Okafor, director of pitching development for the fictional Northfield club, has been asked whether the club can stop sending pitchers to an external marker-based laboratory each winter and rely instead on a markerless system installed in its spring-training complex and, eventually, in affiliate stadiums. The vendor's sales deck cites a peer-reviewed study and describes the markerless system as “validated against the gold standard.” The club's biomechanist, Luis Ferreira, has been asked to brief the department on what that study actually establishes. Okafor wants a recommendation in two weeks; the external laboratory's winter booking deadline falls in three.

Ferreira's first observation is that “validated” is not a property of a system. A study validates particular variables, measured in particular conditions, against a particular reference, for a particular purpose. His briefing therefore begins with the study itself.
The study

Fleisig and colleagues, at a long-established pitching biomechanics laboratory, set out to compare pitching kinematics measured with a markerless and a marker-based system. Thirty pitchers, with a mean age of about 17 years, threw fastballs while both systems recorded simultaneously: a nine-camera markerless system and a twelve-camera marker-based system, both sampling at 240 Hz. In all, 275 fastballs were analyzed. Because the same pitches were recorded by both systems at the same time, differences between the systems cannot be explained by the athlete throwing differently.

For the time-series variables analyzed, agreement between the two systems' waveforms was high, with coefficients of multiple correlation from 0.88 to 0.97: the movement patterns rose and fell together through the delivery. Discrete values, however, differed systematically between systems for several kinematic parameters. The authors concluded that the two systems produced similar patterns but that, given the differences, a separate database of normative ranges should be established for each system.

Ferreira notes what the abstract-level record does and does not let him say. He can say how many pitchers and pitches were analyzed, how the systems were configured, the range of waveform agreement and the authors' recommendation. He should not quote specific variable-by-variable differences unless he reads them from the full paper, and he should not assume which commercial markerless product was used unless the paper names it. The vendor's deck implies that this study validated its current software; Ferreira cannot confirm that the system, model version or camera layout match.
What the department is tempted to conclude

Three readings circulate in the department before the briefing. Okafor's assistant reads the CMC values as proof that the systems are interchangeable. A pitching coach, Marisol Reyes, reads the recommendation of separate norms as proof that the markerless system is inaccurate. A data analyst, Priya Nair, reads the study as irrelevant, because the club wants in-game measurement and the study was done in a laboratory with adolescents.

Each reading takes one feature of the study and stretches it. High CMC shows similar shapes, not equal values; separate norms acknowledge systematic differences between two imperfect systems, not which one is closer to the bone; and a laboratory study of younger pitchers is exactly where a concurrent comparison must start, even if it cannot settle the in-game question.
The surrounding evidence

Ferreira's briefing also places the study among later work. Aguinaldo and colleagues recorded 18 collegiate pitchers simultaneously with a marker-based reference, an in-stadium system and a portable markerless system, reporting mean per-joint position errors of roughly 52–57 mm, the best agreement for stride length and the least for shoulder rotation. Lerch and colleagues compared within-pitcher variability between laboratory marker-based and in-game markerless data, finding it similar for most variables but larger in-game for maximum shoulder external rotation and elbow flexion at that instant, and noting large differences in means; different pitchers were measured in each setting.
For hitting, Ferreira found no peer-reviewed agreement study of markerless swing kinematics. That matters because the club also wants to use the system for hitters.
The tension

The external laboratory offers continuity: five winters of data on many of the club's pitchers, processed with one model. The markerless system offers scale, in-game data and lower cost per athlete. Switching would break every pitcher's longitudinal series, because a marker-based baseline cannot be compared with a markerless follow-up without a correction that applies at the group level, not reliably to individuals. Running both for a year would cost more but would generate the club's own agreement data on its own athletes. Reyes worries that coaches will see markerless shoulder values several degrees different from the laboratory values they know and lose trust; Nair worries that waiting a year means another season without in-game data.
Okafor asks Ferreira for three things: a fair summary of what the study shows, a list of what it does not show, and a recommendation that someone outside biomechanics can act on.

Okafor adds a constraint of her own. The club's pitching coaches have spent five years setting targets in laboratory units — a layback range here, a trunk-tilt range there — and they will read any markerless number against those ranges whether or not they are told not to. Ferreira realizes that his briefing has two audiences: the executives who must decide, and the coaches who will live with whatever numbers appear on their screens. He decides that whatever he recommends must say plainly which numbers can be compared with which, and must show one worked example of what goes wrong if they are not.

Ferreira's draft list of what the study does not establish runs to five items: agreement in games; agreement for professional adults; agreement for the vendor's current model and camera layout; agreement for hitting; and any link between either system's values and performance or injury. He suspects the list is too long to be useful and too important to shorten. He also suspects the most consequential issue is not in the study at all — it is whether the club will ever compare one system's numbers with the other's.

exhibits.note: Synthetic data. Assumptions: the pitcher's true value is constant; the markerless system reads 8° lower than the laboratory system for this variable; each system's typical error is about 2°. The −9° 'change' is almost entirely system offset.
