The vendor's software version differs from whatever version, if any, was used in the published study.
Coaches currently use laboratory values to set individual targets.
questions: Summarize the study's design and main findings in three sentences that a non-specialist executive could not misread.
What does a CMC of 0.88–0.97 establish, and what additional statistic would you need before comparing an individual pitcher's values across systems?
Which features of the sample and setting limit generalization to professional pitchers measured in games? Which later studies address part of that gap, and how well?
What does the study not establish about hitting, about current vendor software, and about performance or injury?
Should the club run both systems for a year? State what that year would need to measure to change your answer.

perspectives.title: Continuity first
perspectives.text: Keep the laboratory this winter and add the markerless system in parallel on the same throws for a subset of pitchers. The published study shows the systems differ in discrete values; the club's own simultaneous data are the only way to estimate bias and limits of agreement for its athletes, software version and variables. Switching without them sacrifices five years of longitudinal series for a correction that is valid only on average.

perspectives.title: Switch, but never mix
perspectives.text: Adopt the markerless system now and treat this season as a new baseline. The study's own recommendation — separate norms per system — is a licence to build a markerless series, not a reason to wait. The error is not changing systems; it is comparing across them. Freeze laboratory values as history, stop referencing them in targets, and estimate the markerless system's typical error in the club's setting before flagging change.

perspectives.title: Validate the purpose, not the system
perspectives.text: Neither the study nor the vendor answers the club's real question, which is whether in-game values can detect changes of the size coaches care about. Define two or three decisions, estimate the system's in-game typical error and MDC for those variables, and adopt it only for variables where the MDC is smaller than the change of interest. Keep hitting out of scope until agreement for swing kinematics is shown.

case.application: The same critique applies to any measurement claim in player development: ask which variables were validated, against what reference, in what athletes and setting, with what statistics, and for what decision. A study can be well designed, honestly reported and still not support the use a vendor or a colleague proposes. The discipline is to separate what the evidence establishes from what it is being used to justify.

questions.prompt: Laboratory A reports a pitcher's peak shoulder external rotation as 178°; Laboratory B, testing him a week later, reports 164°. Both have sub-millimetre calibration residuals. Which question should you ask first?

options.text: Which laboratory has more cameras?
Did the laboratories use the same humerus-relative-to-thorax rotation sequence and glenohumeral joint-centre method?
Was the pitcher's velocity higher in Laboratory A?
Which laboratory's residuals were smaller?

questions.explanation: Joint angles are computed through modelling choices: the rotation sequence and joint-centre estimate change reported shoulder rotation substantially. If those differ, the values are on different scales and the 14° gap may reflect definitions rather than the pitcher. Calibration residuals and camera counts concern reconstruction, the smallest error in the chain.

optionFeedback.a: Camera count affects occlusion and reconstruction, which are rarely the main source of cross-laboratory differences in joint angles.
optionFeedback.c: Velocity is worth knowing, but definitions must be shared before any change can be interpreted.
optionFeedback.d: Both residuals are already sub-millimetre; reconstruction is not the likely source of a 14° difference.

questions.prompt: Select every statement supported by the peer-reviewed markerless pitching studies covered this week.

options.text: Simultaneous capture of the same fastballs showed high waveform agreement between a markerless and a marker system.
The authors of that comparison recommended separate normative ranges for each system.
An in-stadium Hawk-Eye system was shown to agree with marker-based capture within 1° for shoulder rotation.
Within-pitcher variability was similar between in-game markerless and laboratory marker-based data for most, but not all, variables studied.
Markerless systems have been shown to be more accurate than marker systems for humeral rotation.

questions.explanation: Fleisig et al. (2022) reported CMC 0.88–0.97 and recommended system-specific norms; Lerch et al. (2025) found similar variability for eight of ten variables. Aguinaldo et al. (2025) found shoulder rotational variables agreed least, with per-joint position errors of about 52–57 mm; no study established that markerless capture is more accurate than marker capture.

optionFeedback.c: Aguinaldo et al. found shoulder rotation agreed least; no 1° agreement was reported.
optionFeedback.e: Agreement studies compare two imperfect systems; they cannot show which is closer to bone motion.

questions.prompt: What is the most important limitation of the validation claim in this fictional abstract?

stimulus.text: Fictional abstract. “We validated a markerless product we call System Z against marker-based capture in 12 recreational adults walking on a treadmill, recorded simultaneously at 120 Hz. Knee and hip flexion waveforms showed excellent agreement (CMC 0.95–0.98), and peak values were strongly correlated with the reference (r = 0.91–0.96). We conclude that System Z is valid for biomechanical assessment of athletes, including throwing.” Two authors are employees of the company that sells System Z.

options.text: The sample is too large.
Waveform similarity and correlation do not show that peak values agree; no bias or limits of agreement are reported for the variables a user would act on.
Gait is a more demanding test than pitching.
Sampling at 120 Hz is faster than necessary.

questions.explanation: CMC and correlation describe similarity of shape and ranking. A system can match patterns and rank athletes well while reading peak values many degrees off. A user comparing individual values needs the bias and limits of agreement for the discrete variables, in the task of interest, and the conflict of interest should be noted.

optionFeedback.a: Twelve participants is small, not large.
optionFeedback.c: Walking is slower and more planar than pitching; agreement in gait is an upper bound for throwing.
optionFeedback.d: 120 Hz is slow for pitching events; it is a further limitation, not an advantage.

questions.prompt: Which interpretation is best supported?

stimulus.text: Synthetic. A pitcher's arm-worn sensor reports average fastball “elbow torque” of 72 N·m this week versus 66 N·m last week. Mound force plates show lead-leg peak vertical force up from 1.9 to 2.1 body weights, and his average fastball velocity is up 1.2 mph. A staff member writes: “UCL load up 9% — reduce volume.”

options.text: The pitcher's ligament load rose 9%, so his volume should be cut.

Estimated net elbow moment rose by an amount that may be within the sensor's error, alongside higher velocity; describe it, check the error, and leave load decisions to the medical and performance staff.
The sensor is broken because its values are lower than laboratory torque.
The force-plate increase proves the arm torque increase is real.

questions.explanation: The wearable estimates a net joint moment from one segment's kinematics and a model; it does not measure ligament load, and its published comparison found values correlated with but substantially lower than laboratory torque. Higher velocity is associated with higher estimated torque. Without the sensor's within-pitcher typical error, a 6 N·m change cannot be called real, and loading decisions are clinical.

optionFeedback.a: Net joint moment is not ligament load, and the change has not been shown to exceed measurement error.
optionFeedback.c: A consistent negative bias versus laboratory torque is expected from the published comparison; it does not mean the sensor is broken.
optionFeedback.d: Force plates measure a different quantity; agreement in direction does not validate the size of the torque change.

questions.prompt: In a test–retest study of peak lead-knee flexion at ball release, the standard deviation of the session-to-session differences is 4.2°. What is the typical error?
questions.explanation: Each difference score carries the error of two measurements, so its variance is twice the single-measurement error variance. Dividing the SD of differences by √2 gives the typical error of a single measurement.

questions.prompt: A field system's game-to-game typical error for a pitcher's peak shoulder external rotation is 3.0°. What is the MDC95?
questions.explanation: The change score between two occasions has error √2 × TE; multiplying by 1.96 gives the change that a stable athlete would exceed only 5% of the time. A change smaller than about 8.3° cannot be distinguished from error with 95% confidence.

questions.prompt: In a Bland–Altman comparison of two systems, the mean difference (System F − System L) is 6.0° and the SD of the differences is 3.5°. What is the upper 95% limit of agreement?
questions.explanation: Limits of agreement are bias ± 1.96 SD of the paired differences. For an individual measurement, System F is expected to read between about 0.9° below and 12.9° above System L, which is far too wide to swap the systems for decisions about individual athletes.

questions.prompt: What is the central flaw in this argument?

stimulus.text: “After our sequencing program, the hitter's average Statcast bat speed rose 1.8 mph and his attack angle rose 3°. The tracking data therefore confirm that his pelvis now leads his trunk by more, which is exactly what the program targeted.”

options.text: Bat tracking cannot measure bat speed.
Bat speed and attack angle describe the bat's motion; they cannot show how the body sequenced segments, so they cannot confirm a change in the kinematic sequence.
The hitter's sample of swings is too large.
Attack angle should be measured at the start of the swing.

questions.explanation: Tracking-derived metrics are outputs about the implement. A higher bat speed is consistent with many changes — or none — in pelvis and trunk sequencing, and attack angle also depends on pitch location. Claims about body kinematics require body measurement, from a validated system.

optionFeedback.a: Bat speed is a defined, tracked property of the sweet spot at contact.
optionFeedback.c: More swings improve the estimate of the bat metrics; the problem is what those metrics can represent.
optionFeedback.d: Statcast defines attack angle at contact; the definition is not the flaw.

questions.prompt: Rank these forms of evidence for the claim “the field markerless system can replace the laboratory system for measuring an individual pitcher's peak shoulder external rotation,” strongest first.

options.text: Correlation (r = 0.95) between the systems' values in a different sample of pitchers, each measured once by each system on separate days
Bland–Altman bias and limits of agreement from simultaneous capture of the same pitches in the club's own pitchers
A vendor press release stating accuracy “within 3°”
High waveform CMC from simultaneous capture in a published study, without discrete-value agreement statistics

questions.explanation: Simultaneous capture with bias and limits of agreement in the target athletes directly answers the interchangeability question. Simultaneous CMC removes athlete differences but addresses shape rather than values. A correlation across separate days confounds system with day-to-day variation and cannot establish agreement. A press release reports no methods.

questions.prompt: Which is the best next move?

stimulus.text: Synthetic. January laboratory value: 176°. Field markerless value in February: 168°; in April, after a drill block: 166°. Agreement data: field − laboratory bias −8.0°, limits −13.5° to −2.5°. Field typical error 2.1° (MDC95 ≈ 5.8°). The pitching coordinator wants to tell the player that the drills reduced his layback by 10°.

options.text: Report a 10° reduction in layback caused by the drill block.
Report that laboratory-to-field comparisons are not interpretable for individuals, compare like with like, and schedule a same-system retest.
Average the laboratory and field values to cancel the bias.
Discard the field system because it reads lower.

questions.explanation: The baseline and follow-up come from different systems with a −8° bias and wide limits, so most of the apparent 10° change is offset. Within the field system, the change from the February field value is 2°, below its MDC95 of about 5.8°. The defensible action is to compare within one system and retest.

optionFeedback.a: This attributes a cross-system offset to the drill.
optionFeedback.c: Averaging across systems produces a number that belongs to neither and does not remove the bias from the comparison.
optionFeedback.d: A known, stable bias does not disqualify a system for within-system monitoring.

questions.prompt: Why is surface EMG amplitude during arm acceleration not a valid measure of how much force the muscle produced?

options.text: Because EMG measures only fine-wire signals.
Because amplitude depends on electrode placement, crosstalk and normalization, and the EMG–force relationship changes with muscle length and velocity in dynamic tasks.
Because EMG cannot be filtered.
Because muscles are electrically silent during ballistic movements.

questions.explanation: Surface EMG records electrical activity under the electrode, contaminated by crosstalk and affected by tissue and placement. Even when normalized, its relation to force holds reasonably only in controlled isometric conditions; in throwing, muscle length, shortening velocity and electromechanical delay break the mapping.

optionFeedback.a: Surface EMG is a distinct method from fine-wire EMG and is widely used.
optionFeedback.c: EMG is routinely band-pass filtered, rectified and smoothed.
optionFeedback.d: Muscles are highly active during ballistic tasks; the issue is interpreting amplitude as force.

questions.prompt: A hitting coordinator wants to use the stadium's in-game markerless system to detect whether a hitter's pelvis-rotation timing changed after a two-week program. In 120–180 words, state what you would need to know or measure before accepting a reported change, and what the current peer-reviewed evidence on markerless hitting does and does not provide.
questions.modelAnswer: I would need the system's within-hitter typical error for this timing variable in games, estimated from repeated at-bats with no intervention, and from it the MDC95; the change must exceed that. Timing resolution matters: at the system's frame rate, event detection is uncertain by up to half a frame, so changes of a few milliseconds may be undetectable. I would also confirm no software or camera change occurred between periods and compare against pitch type and location, which alter swing timing. The peer-reviewed evidence includes a large in-game observational study relating hip–shoulder separation to bat speed within and between Division I batters, which shows such data can be analyzed at scale, but I found no peer-reviewed study validating markerless swing kinematics against a laboratory reference. So I can track change within the system once its error is known, but not claim the absolute values are accurate.

levels: 0 — not mentioned
1 — mentions error without a same-system, in-game estimate
2 — requires within-hitter typical error and MDC in the setting of use
0 — not addressed
1 — names one (frame rate, software change, pitch context)
2 — names frame-rate limits and at least one other confound
0 — claims none exists or that it is validated
1 — partly accurate
2 — notes the in-game observational study and the absence of a peer-reviewed agreement study

reserve.prompt: A pitcher cannot perform a controlled shoulder range-of-motion movement before testing. Which joint-centre approach is more practical, and what is its main cost?

options.text: Functional; it requires no movement
Predictive (regression from landmarks); it inherits the population and imaging assumptions of its equations
Functional; it cannot locate ball joints
Predictive; it requires biplanar radiography

reserve.explanation: Predictive methods need only a static trial with landmarks, so they work when a calibration movement is not possible, but they apply population equations that may not fit the individual. Functional methods need sufficient range of motion and are sensitive to soft-tissue artifact during that movement.

optionFeedback.a: Functional methods require the very movement the pitcher cannot perform.
optionFeedback.c: Functional methods are designed for ball joints.
optionFeedback.d: Predictive methods use palpated landmarks, not radiography.

reserve.prompt: Assume a bat–ball contact lasting 1 ms. On average, how many video frames fall within contact at 480 frames per second?
reserve.working: Frame interval = 1/480 s = 2.083 ms; expected frames in 1 ms = 1 / 2.083 = 0.48.
reserve.explanation: Expected frames during an event equal its duration times the frame rate. At 480 Hz fewer than half of swings will have any frame during a 1 ms contact.

reserve.prompt: A gyroscope has an uncorrected bias of 0.2°/s. How much orientation error accumulates over 90 s of integration?
reserve.explanation: Integrating a constant rate bias produces orientation error that grows linearly with time, which is why sensor fusion uses gravity and magnetic references and why throwing sensors re-reference frequently.

reserve.prompt: A study reports ICC = 0.91 for a markerless variable in a sample of youth to professional pitchers. What does this mainly tell you?

options.text: The variable can detect a 2° change in one professional pitcher.
Measurement error is small relative to the between-pitcher spread in that heterogeneous sample, which inflates ICC.
The markerless system agrees with marker capture.
The ICC form does not matter at this value.

reserve.explanation: ICC is the ratio of between-subject variance to total variance; a sample spanning youth to professional athletes has large between-subject variance, so ICC is high even with moderate error. Detecting change in one athlete requires the typical error and MDC; agreement with another system requires a Bland–Altman analysis; and the form must always be reported.

optionFeedback.a: Individual change detection depends on the typical error, which ICC alone does not give.
optionFeedback.c: Reliability within one system says nothing about agreement with another.
optionFeedback.d: Model, type and definition change ICC values and must be reported.

assignment.title: Measurement System Fitness-for-Purpose Memo

brief.text: You lead applied biomechanics for a fictional professional club. The development department proposes buying System F, a fictional multi-camera markerless system sampling at 300 frames per second, for the club's spring complex and two affiliate stadiums. Its stated purpose is narrow: flag, for coach review, any in-season change in a player's mechanics that is large enough to matter. Coaches have told you the size of change they would act on for five variables. The vendor's materials say System F is “validated.” Your own staff ran a pilot: simultaneous capture against the club's laboratory marker system, and repeated in-game measurement of stable athletes. Write the memo that recommends whether, and for which variables, System F is fit for this purpose.

brief.caption: Pilot validation data for System F (synthetic)
headers: In-game typical error (mean of ≥ 10 pitches or swings)
rows: Pitching: trunk forward tilt at release
Hitting: stride-foot contact to peak pelvis velocity
brief.note: Synthetic data for a fictional system and club. Pilot: 14 pitchers and 12 hitters for agreement (laboratory, simultaneous capture); 20 athletes for in-game typical error. MDC95 = 1.96 × √2 × typical error.

brief.text: Use the week's statistics explicitly. Distinguish what the pilot shows about agreement (needed only if you will compare with laboratory values) from what it shows about in-game reliability (needed for within-system monitoring). Note the frame interval at 300 Hz when you judge the timing variable. State what the peer-reviewed literature does and does not add, especially for hitting, and do not treat the vendor's word “validated” as evidence.

assignment.deliverable: A 900–1,300-word memo recommending, variable by variable, whether System F is fit to flag in-season mechanical change, with conditions and a monitoring plan.

template.heading: Recommendation
template.guidance: Three to five sentences: adopt, adopt for some variables, or do not adopt; for which purpose; the main condition.

template.heading: The decision and its measurement requirement
template.guidance: Restate the purpose and translate it into a requirement: the system's in-game MDC must be smaller than the change coaches would act on, and comparisons must stay within one system.

template.heading: Variable-by-variable assessment
template.guidance: For each of the five variables, compare MDC95 with the change of interest, comment on bias and limits of agreement, and conclude fit / conditionally fit / not fit. Address frame-rate limits for the timing variable.

template.heading: What the evidence does and does not establish
template.guidance: Place the pilot alongside the published markerless literature (pitching agreement studies; the state of hitting evidence). Separate vendor claims from peer-reviewed findings.

template.heading: Risks and safeguards
template.guidance: Software updates, camera changes between stadiums, mixing systems, coaches' expectations from laboratory values, and any temptation to read loading or injury meaning into the outputs.

template.heading: Monitoring and re-evaluation plan
template.guidance: How you will version-stamp data, re-estimate typical error each season, and what result would change your recommendation.

levels.label: Exemplary
levels.descriptor: Uses MDC versus change-of-interest for every variable, distinguishes bias and limits of agreement from typical error, and explains which matters for within-system monitoring.

levels.label: Proficient
levels.descriptor: Uses MDC and agreement statistics correctly for most variables with minor confusions.

levels.label: Developing
levels.descriptor: Uses some statistics but conflates agreement with reliability or relies on ICC-like reasoning.

levels.label: Beginning
levels.descriptor: Does not use the pilot statistics or misinterprets them.

levels.label: Exemplary
levels.descriptor: Reaches defensible, differentiated conclusions (e.g., fit for knee flexion, borderline for trunk tilt, not fit for shoulder ER or pelvis velocity) and handles the timing variable's frame interval.

levels.label: Proficient
levels.descriptor: Differentiated conclusions with one weakly justified call.

levels.label: Developing
levels.descriptor: Treats the system as wholly fit or unfit without variable-level reasoning.

levels.label: Beginning
levels.descriptor: No variable-level judgement.

levels.label: Exemplary
levels.descriptor: Accurately represents published markerless pitching agreement studies and the absence of peer-reviewed hitting agreement studies; treats vendor claims as claims.

levels.label: Proficient
levels.descriptor: Mostly accurate, with a minor overstatement.

levels.label: Developing
levels.descriptor: Overstates or understates the literature in a way that affects the recommendation.

levels.label: Beginning
levels.descriptor: Relies on the vendor's description or misstates the research.

levels.label: Exemplary
levels.descriptor: Specific safeguards for software versions, cross-system comparison and loading misinterpretation, with a re-evaluation trigger.

levels.label: Proficient
levels.descriptor: Sound safeguards with limited specificity.

levels.label: Developing
levels.descriptor: Generic risks without safeguards.

levels.label: Beginning
levels.descriptor: Risks not addressed.

levels.label: Exemplary
levels.descriptor: A non-specialist can act on the recommendation from the first section; terms defined; no hedging beyond what the evidence requires.

levels.label: Proficient
levels.descriptor: Clear with minor jargon.

prompts: Name one biomechanical or tracking number you have relied on in a decision. What was its typical error in the setting where it was collected, and did you know it at the time?
Where in your own environment are values from two different systems, or two software versions, being compared as if they were on one scale?
Which instrument in this week's lessons would you trust most for a within-athlete decision about hitters, and which least? What would change your ranking?
How would you explain to a coach, in two sentences, why a 5° change in a pitcher's layback might not be a change at all?

review.front: What does a marker-based system measure directly, and what does it model?
review.back: It measures 3D positions of skin markers by triangulation; segment orientation, joint centres, joint angles and moments are modelled.

review.front: What is the dominant error in skin-marker estimates of bone motion?
review.back: Soft-tissue artifact: skin and muscle moving relative to bone. It is subject- and task-specific and worst for long-axis rotations.

review.front: Functional versus predictive joint centres: one advantage and one cost of each.
review.back: Functional: individualized, but needs adequate range of motion and is sensitive to soft-tissue artifact. Predictive: needs only a static trial, but applies population equations.

review.front: Why does a clean angle signal produce a noisy angular acceleration?
review.back: Each differentiation multiplies noise by roughly the sampling rate; at 240 Hz, 0.8° angle noise becomes hundreds of °/s in velocity and over 10⁵ °/s² in acceleration unless filtered.

review.front: What is a markerless keypoint, and why is it not a joint centre?
review.back: A network's estimate of a labelled visual point; training labels are human visual judgements of joint locations, not anatomical centres.

review.front: What did Fleisig et al. (2022) find and recommend?
review.back: On 275 fastballs from 30 pitchers captured simultaneously, waveforms agreed (CMC 0.88–0.97) but discrete values differed systematically; separate norms per system.

review.front: What exists, peer-reviewed, on in-game markerless hitting (as of Nov 2026)?
review.back: Large observational work (e.g., 3,958 swings by 247 Division I batters relating separation to bat speed); no peer-reviewed markerless–marker agreement study of swing kinematics was found.

review.front: How is centre of pressure computed, and when is it unreliable?
review.back: From the plate's moments divided by vertical force; unreliable when vertical force is small, so a force threshold is applied.

review.front: Why do IMU orientation and position drift?
review.back: They are integrals of angular velocity and acceleration; constant biases grow linearly (orientation) or quadratically (position) with time.

review.front: What does a wearable elbow-torque sensor output?
review.back: A modelled net elbow moment from one segment's kinematics plus assumed arm properties; correlated with but lower than laboratory torque in a published comparison; not ligament load.

review.front: Why is EMG amplitude not muscle force?
review.back: It reflects electrical activity under the electrode, affected by placement, crosstalk and normalization; in dynamic tasks length and velocity change force for the same activation.

review.front: Degrees per frame for a 7,000°/s rotation at 240 Hz?
Statcast attack angle — definition.
review.back: The vertical direction in which the bat's sweet spot is travelling at contact (or projected contact on a miss).

review.front: A 1-frame synchronization offset at 240 Hz with the bat at 32 m/s displaces the bat by about how much?
Typical error and MDC95 formulas.
review.back: TE = SD of test–retest differences / √2; MDC95 = 1.96 × √2 × TE ≈ 2.77 × TE.

review.front: Why can ICC be high while a measure cannot detect change in one athlete?
review.back: ICC is between-subject variance over total variance; a heterogeneous sample inflates it without reducing the typical error.

review.front: What do Bland–Altman limits of agreement tell you that correlation cannot?
review.back: The bias and the range within which 95% of individual differences between methods fall, in measurement units.

preview.text: This week gave you the instruments and the arithmetic of error. Week 3 applies them to the lower body and trunk in pitching: ground reaction forces from mound plates, pelvis–trunk sequencing from 3D capture and energy-flow analyses built on inverse dynamics — each of which inherits the joint-centre, filtering and synchronization issues you studied here. Week 7 returns to tracked bat metrics and collision physics, and Week 12 extends this week's reliability statistics into the design of intervention studies, where the question becomes not only whether a change is real but whether something caused it.

intro.text: This diagnostic has 28 questions, four in each of the course's seven domains: functional anatomy, vector and rotational mathematics, kinematics, kinetics, motor control, measurement science and research literacy. Expect it to take about 30 minutes. Some items are calculations; a basic calculator is fine, but answer without looking anything up.

Its purpose is to identify prerequisite gaps before you start. The course assumes a working command of vectors, rotational mechanics and measurement error, and the diagnostic shows quickly where a short refresher would make the lessons easier to follow.

The diagnostic is never graded and never counts toward any mark. It does not block you from starting the course: every lesson stays open whatever you score. Several items are stretch-level, so missing some is expected.

After you submit, each answer comes with an explanation and each domain shows a short interpretation. Where your answers suggest a gap, the interpretation names an optional refresher: what to review and roughly how, before or alongside the relevant lessons.

questions.prompt: A person holds the forearm horizontal with the elbow flexed to 90°. A hand-held load produces a downward force of 30 N at 0.35 m from the elbow joint center. The elbow flexors act at a perpendicular moment arm of 0.04 m. Ignoring the weight of the forearm and any co-contraction of the extensors, what flexor force (in newtons) is needed to hold the position statically?
questions.working: Sum of moments about the elbow = 0: F_muscle × 0.04 m = 30 N × 0.35 m = 10.5 N·m. F_muscle = 10.5 / 0.04 = 262.5 N.
questions.explanation: Static equilibrium requires the flexor moment to equal the load moment about the elbow. Because the flexors' moment arm is about one ninth of the load's, the muscle force is roughly nine times the load. This is the usual arrangement in the limbs: short muscle moment arms trade force for range and speed at the distal end of the segment.

questions.prompt: Which statement best describes the force–velocity relationship of skeletal muscle?

options.text: Muscle force is independent of contraction velocity once the muscle is fully activated
Concentric force falls as shortening velocity increases, and eccentric force can exceed isometric force
Muscle produces its greatest force at its maximum shortening velocity
Eccentric force is always lower than isometric force because the cross-bridges are being pulled apart

questions.explanation: In concentric (shortening) contractions the force a fully activated muscle can produce falls as shortening velocity rises, approaching zero at maximum shortening velocity. In eccentric (lengthening) contractions force can exceed the isometric maximum. This is one reason fast segments in throwing and swinging depend on energy delivered from other segments rather than on their own muscles alone.

optionFeedback.a: Activation sets the available force, but at full activation force still depends strongly on velocity.
optionFeedback.c: The reverse: force approaches zero as shortening velocity approaches its maximum, and peak mechanical power occurs at intermediate velocities.
optionFeedback.d: Lengthening contractions typically produce forces above the isometric maximum.

questions.prompt: Which statements about muscle and joint function are correct? Select all that apply.

options.text: After ball release, posterior shoulder muscles act largely eccentrically to decelerate the arm
Active muscle force depends on sarcomere length, peaking near an optimal length
Two-joint (biarticular) muscles can transfer mechanical energy between the joints they cross
A muscle's moment arm about a joint is constant through the joint's range of motion
Type II muscle fibers have a lower maximum shortening velocity than type I fibers

questions.explanation: Posterior shoulder muscles work eccentrically to decelerate the arm after ball release, active force depends on sarcomere length, and two-joint muscles can redistribute mechanical energy between joints. Muscle moment arms change with joint angle, and fast-twitch (type II) fibers shorten faster than slow-twitch fibers, not slower.

optionFeedback.a: Correct. Deceleration requires the muscles to absorb energy while lengthening.
optionFeedback.b: Correct. This is the length–tension relationship.
optionFeedback.c: Correct. A biarticular muscle can shorten little while one joint extends and the other flexes, moving energy between segments.
optionFeedback.d: Incorrect. Moment arms vary with joint angle, often substantially.
optionFeedback.e: Incorrect. Type II fibers have the higher maximum shortening velocity.

stimulus.text: An athlete performs two maximal vertical jumps. In a squat jump she starts from a held half-squat and pushes upward. In a countermovement jump she starts standing, dips quickly to the same depth and pushes upward without pausing. The countermovement jump is consistently higher.

questions.prompt: Which explanation of this difference is most defensible?

options.text: The countermovement increases the athlete's maximal muscle strength for that one jump
The countermovement jump is higher only because of the stretch reflex
The quick dip lets muscles build force before the upward phase begins, and tendons return some stored elastic energy; the reflex share is debated
Energy stored in the dip creates extra work beyond what the muscles and tendons supply

questions.explanation: The countermovement lets the muscles reach a high active state and force before the upward (concentric) phase begins, and stretched tendons return part of the stored elastic energy. The size of any stretch-reflex contribution is debated. The difference does not show that the muscles became stronger, and work done is not created from nothing.

optionFeedback.a: Maximal strength does not change within one movement; what changes is how much force is available at the start of the concentric phase.
optionFeedback.b: The reflex may contribute, but its share is contested and it is not the sole mechanism.
optionFeedback.d: Energy is conserved. Elastic recoil returns energy that muscles put into the tendons during the dip; it does not create extra work.

questions.prompt: Two segment-direction vectors are a = (3, 4, 0) and b = (4, 0, 3), in the same units. Using the dot product, what is the angle between them in degrees? Round to one decimal place.
questions.explanation: The dot product equals the product of the magnitudes and the cosine of the included angle, so the angle follows from the normalized dot product. This is how the angle between two segment axes is computed from marker-derived vectors, independent of any coordinate sequence.

questions.prompt: In a right-handed coordinate system, a force F = (0, 20, 0) N acts at position r = (0.5, 0, 0) m relative to a joint center. What is the moment M = r × F about the joint center?

options.text: (0, 10, 0) N·m, because the moment points along the force

questions.explanation: M = r × F = (r_y F_z − r_z F_y, r_z F_x − r_x F_z, r_x F_y − r_y F_x) = (0, 0, 0.5 × 20) = (0, 0, 10) N·m. By the right-hand rule, curling the fingers from +x toward +y points the thumb along +z. The order matters: F × r would give the opposite sign.

optionFeedback.b: This is F × r. The cross product is anticommutative, so reversing the order flips the sign.
optionFeedback.c: The moment is perpendicular to both r (x) and F (y), so it must lie along z.
optionFeedback.d: A moment is perpendicular to the force and the moment arm, never parallel to the force.

questions.prompt: A rigid segment rotates about a fixed axis at 1,000°/s. What is the linear (tangential) speed, in m/s, of a point 0.6 m from the axis? Round to two decimal places.
questions.explanation: The relation v = ωr holds only when ω is expressed in radians per second, because the radian is defined as arc length divided by radius. Using degrees per second directly would overstate the speed by a factor of about 57.3.

questions.prompt: Which statements about describing three-dimensional rotations are correct? Select all that apply.

options.text: Applying the same two finite rotations in a different order generally produces a different final orientation
One orientation can produce different joint-angle values under different Cardan sequences
The angular velocity vector equals the time derivatives of the three Cardan angles, component by component
A proper rotation matrix is orthogonal and has a determinant of +1
A Cardan sequence becomes singular when its first rotation approaches 90°

questions.explanation: Finite rotations about different axes do not commute, so the same orientation yields different angle triplets under different Cardan or Euler sequences, which is why the sequence must be reported. A rotation matrix is orthogonal with determinant +1. The angular velocity vector is not, in general, the time derivative of the three Cardan angles, and the singularity (gimbal lock) occurs when the second rotation approaches ±90°, not the first.

optionFeedback.a: Correct. Finite 3D rotations are not commutative.
optionFeedback.b: Correct. Angle values depend on the sequence, so comparisons across studies need the same convention.
optionFeedback.c: Incorrect. The Cardan-angle rates are measured about non-orthogonal axes; converting them to angular velocity requires a transformation that depends on the current angles.
optionFeedback.d: Correct. Orthogonality preserves lengths and angles; determinant +1 excludes reflections.
optionFeedback.e: Incorrect. The singularity occurs when the second (middle) rotation approaches ±90°, aligning the first and third axes.

questions.prompt: A ball leaves the bat at 45 m/s with a launch angle of 30° above horizontal. Ignoring air resistance and spin, and assuming it lands at the height it was struck, how far does it travel horizontally, in meters? Use g = 9.81 m/s². Round to the nearest meter.
questions.explanation: In a vacuum the range is v² sin(2θ) / g. The answer is far longer than real batted balls of this speed travel, because drag and the lift from backspin reshape the trajectory substantially. The idealized model is a reference point that shows how much of real ball flight is aerodynamics.

stimulus.text: Marker position data for a hand marker, captured at 240 Hz, look smooth when plotted. After two finite-difference differentiations, the hand's acceleration trace is dominated by large, rapid spikes that make peak acceleration impossible to identify.

questions.prompt: What is the most likely cause, and the appropriate response?

options.text: The hand truly accelerates in rapid spikes; report the largest spike as peak acceleration
Differentiation amplifies small high-frequency position noise; filter the data with a justified, reported cutoff before or while differentiating
Sampling at 240 Hz is too fast; resample to 60 Hz and differentiate again
Acceleration cannot be computed from position data and must always be measured with an accelerometer

questions.explanation: Measurement noise in position data is mostly high frequency, and differentiation multiplies each frequency component by its frequency, so noise is amplified once for velocity and again for acceleration. The standard response is to low-pass filter (choosing and reporting the cutoff, for example from residual analysis) before or while differentiating. Raising the sampling rate alone does not remove noise and can make finite-difference noise worse.

optionFeedback.a: The spikes are a signal-processing artifact, not physiology. Reporting them would grossly overstate peak acceleration.
optionFeedback.c: Downsampling discards information and can alias fast events; the issue is noise amplification, not sampling rate as such.
optionFeedback.d: Acceleration is routinely and validly derived from filtered position data; accelerometers have their own errors.

questions.prompt: In laboratory studies of professional pitchers, rank these peak angular velocities from largest (first) to smallest (last).

options.text: Pelvis (axial) rotation
Upper-trunk (axial) rotation
Elbow extension
Shoulder internal rotation

questions.explanation: Published three-dimensional studies of professional pitchers report peak pelvis rotation velocity of roughly 600–700°/s, upper-trunk rotation around 1,100–1,200°/s, elbow extension around 2,300–2,500°/s and shoulder internal rotation around 7,000°/s or more. The increase from proximal to distal segments reflects transfer of energy along the chain to lighter segments. Exact values vary by laboratory, marker model and definition, so compare only within one method.

optionFeedback.a: Smallest: the heavy pelvis rotates the slowest of the four.
optionFeedback.b: Faster than the pelvis but far slower than the arm joints.
optionFeedback.c: Fast, but typically about a third of shoulder internal rotation velocity.
optionFeedback.d: Largest: among the fastest joint motions recorded in human movement.

questions.prompt: A report states that a pitcher's peak "elbow angular velocity" was 2,400°/s. Which information is most necessary to interpret the number?

options.text: The pitcher's release velocity, because elbow angular velocity is proportional to it
Whether the value was measured during a game or a bullpen
Whether it is a joint angular velocity relative to the upper arm or a segment angular velocity in the laboratory frame, about which axis, and how the data were processed
Nothing: angular velocity is a scalar, so 2,400°/s has one meaning

questions.explanation: An elbow value may be a joint (relative) angular velocity of the forearm with respect to the upper arm, about a defined flexion–extension axis, or a segment's angular velocity in the laboratory frame. These can differ greatly in the same pitch. Without the definition, axis convention and processing (marker model, filter cutoff), the number cannot be compared with another report.

optionFeedback.a: Release velocity is related across pitchers but is not a conversion factor for a kinematic definition.
optionFeedback.b: Context matters, but even within one context the definition determines what the number means.
optionFeedback.d: Angular velocity is a vector, and joint versus segment definitions give different values.

questions.prompt: A 0.145 kg baseball arrives at the bat at 40 m/s and leaves in the opposite direction at 45 m/s. Contact lasts 0.7 ms. What is the average force of the bat on the ball during contact, in kilonewtons? Round to one decimal place.
questions.explanation: By the impulse–momentum theorem, average force equals the change in momentum divided by contact time. Because the ball reverses direction, the velocity change is the sum of the two speeds. The very short contact time is why bat–ball forces are so large, and why what happens during contact cannot be steered by the hitter.

questions.prompt: From inverse dynamics, a net joint moment of 80 N·m acts in the same direction as the joint's angular velocity of 600°/s at one instant. What is the joint power, in watts? Round to the nearest watt.
questions.explanation: Joint power is the product of the net joint moment and the joint angular velocity in radians per second. Because the moment and angular velocity have the same sign, power is positive: net mechanical energy is being generated at the joint (often described as concentric dominance). Negative power would mean energy absorption. Net joint power does not identify which muscles did the work.

stimulus.text: A report on two pitchers states: "Pitcher A's peak elbow varus moment was 100 N·m and Pitcher B's was 85 N·m. Pitcher A's ulnar collateral ligament therefore carries about 18% more force, and A's risk of an elbow injury is about 18% higher."

questions.prompt: What is the central flaw in this reasoning?

options.text: It treats a net joint moment as the ligament's own load, and treats load as if it translated proportionally into injury probability
Elbow varus moments cannot be calculated from motion capture data
The percentage is calculated incorrectly; 100 is 15% more than 85
It should have compared shoulder moments, because the shoulder carries the highest loads

questions.explanation: Inverse dynamics yields the net moment of every structure crossing the joint: muscles, ligaments, joint contact and capsule, with co-contraction hidden inside the net value. It does not give the ligament's force, and a load is not a probability of injury, which also depends on tissue capacity, repetitions, recovery and history. Body mass and height also need to be considered before comparing absolute moments.

optionFeedback.b: Elbow varus moments are routinely estimated with inverse dynamics; the issue is interpretation, not calculability.
optionFeedback.c: 100 / 85 = 1.176, so about 18% is arithmetically right. The flaw is conceptual.
optionFeedback.d: Choosing another joint does not fix the confusion between a net moment, tissue load and injury risk.

questions.prompt: An athlete is airborne. Ignoring air resistance, which statements are correct? Select all that apply.

options.text: Whole-body angular momentum about the center of mass stays constant
Pulling the limbs toward the rotation axis increases whole-body angular velocity
Swinging the arms in the air creates new whole-body angular momentum
With zero angular momentum the athlete can still change body orientation through internal movements
Moving the limbs in the air changes the path of the center of mass

questions.explanation: With gravity as the only external force, and gravity acting through the center of mass, whole-body angular momentum about the center of mass is constant and the center of mass follows a parabola set at takeoff. Changing the moment of inertia changes angular velocity. Internal motions cannot create net angular momentum, but they can still change body orientation even when angular momentum is zero, as in the falling-cat problem.

optionFeedback.a: Correct. No external moment acts about the center of mass.
optionFeedback.b: Correct. Angular momentum is conserved, so a smaller moment of inertia means faster rotation.
optionFeedback.c: Incorrect. Arm motion redistributes angular momentum among segments; the total stays the same.
optionFeedback.d: Correct. Sequences of shape changes allow reorientation with zero net angular momentum.
optionFeedback.e: Incorrect. Only external forces change the center-of-mass path; it is fixed at takeoff.

questions.prompt: Across 50 pitches, a pitcher's release point varies little, while shoulder, elbow and trunk angles at release vary more. Deviations in one joint tend to be offset by deviations in another. Which interpretation fits current motor control theory best?

options.text: The joint variability is error the pitcher should eliminate to achieve one correct pattern
The pattern is consistent with motor abundance: variability in directions that do not affect the task goal is tolerated, while compensation stabilizes release
Joint angles cannot vary if release point is consistent, so the data must contain measurement error
Release-point consistency shows the pitcher replays a single stored joint-angle trajectory

questions.explanation: The motor system has more degrees of freedom than the task requires. Variability that leaves the task variable unchanged (here, release location) is often allowed, while variability that would disturb it is corrected or compensated. Covariation among joints that stabilizes the outcome is the signature analyzed with uncontrolled-manifold methods. Joint variability is not by itself an error, and it is not evidence of a skill deficit.

optionFeedback.a: Treating all variability as error ignores that compensatory variability can protect the task outcome.
optionFeedback.c: With redundant joints, many joint configurations reach the same endpoint.
optionFeedback.d: The joint-level variability contradicts a single replayed trajectory.

stimulus.text: A 95 mph (about 42.5 m/s) pitch released about 16.8 m from the front of home plate arrives in roughly 0.40 s. A hitter's swing from initiation to contact takes around 0.15 s, and the delay between a visual event and a corrective motor response is typically 0.1–0.2 s.

questions.prompt: Which conclusion is best supported?

options.text: The hitter can track the ball to the bat and correct the swing continuously until contact
Visual information is irrelevant to hitting at this speed
Only reaction time distinguishes better hitters from weaker ones
The hitter must commit using predictions from early-flight and pre-release information, with limited capacity for late correction

questions.explanation: Visuomotor delays of roughly 100–200 ms, combined with a swing that itself needs about 150 ms or more, leave little time for vision late in flight to change the swing. Hitting therefore relies heavily on prediction: early-flight information, pitcher cues and expectations about pitch type and location. Some late adjustment is possible, so the claim is not that vision is irrelevant late, but that prediction carries much of the load.

optionFeedback.a: Sensorimotor delays make continuous visual correction near contact impossible.
optionFeedback.b: Vision early in flight and before release supplies the information on which prediction depends.
optionFeedback.c: Simple reaction time differs little between elite and less skilled performers; anticipation and pattern use matter more.

questions.prompt: Which statements are consistent with optimal feedback control and internal-model accounts of movement? Select all that apply.

options.text: Deviations that do not affect the task goal tend not to be corrected
A forward model predicts the sensory consequences of a motor command
The nervous system plans one fixed joint trajectory and replays it identically on every attempt
Larger motor commands produce more variable output, which contributes to the speed–accuracy trade-off
Proprioceptive feedback is effectively delay-free, so internal prediction is unnecessary

questions.explanation: Optimal feedback control holds that the nervous system corrects deviations that threaten the task goal and leaves others alone (the minimum intervention principle). State estimation combines forward-model predictions of a command's sensory consequences with delayed, noisy feedback. Motor noise grows with the size of the command, which contributes to the speed–accuracy trade-off. Sensory feedback is never delay-free, and these accounts do not prescribe one fixed joint trajectory.

optionFeedback.a: Correct. This is the minimum intervention principle.
optionFeedback.b: Correct. Forward models help compensate for sensory delay.
optionFeedback.c: Incorrect. Optimal feedback control produces flexible, state-dependent corrections rather than a replayed trajectory.
optionFeedback.d: Correct. This is signal-dependent noise.
optionFeedback.e: Incorrect. Proprioceptive loops still take tens of milliseconds, which is why prediction matters.

stimulus.text: A hitting coach introduces a new cue in a 30-minute session of front-toss. By the end of the session, a hitter's rate of hard contact on front-toss has risen from 35% to 55%. The coach writes: "The cue fixed his swing; he has learned the new pattern." (Synthetic numbers.)

questions.prompt: What is the main weakness in the coach's conclusion?

options.text: Front-toss cannot produce hard contact, so the numbers must be wrong
The improvement is too large to be real and should be ignored
Performance during acquisition was measured, but learning requires delayed retention and transfer tests, for example to live pitching
The coach should have used a larger percentage scale

questions.explanation: The measurements were taken during or immediately after practice under the new cue, which captures temporary performance and possibly short-term adaptation. Learning is a relatively permanent change inferred from delayed retention and from transfer to other conditions, such as live pitching. Without those tests, the gains may fade or fail to appear in games.

optionFeedback.a: Hard contact on front-toss is plausible; the issue is what the measurement can show.
optionFeedback.b: Large practice gains can be real performance changes; they are just not proof of learning.
optionFeedback.d: The scale is irrelevant; the design lacks retention and transfer tests.

questions.prompt: Twenty pitchers each throw a velocity test on two days one week apart, with no training change between. The standard deviation of the between-day difference scores is 2.4 mph. What is the typical error (within-subject standard deviation) in mph? Round to two decimal places.
questions.explanation: When each athlete is measured twice, the difference score contains error from both trials, so its standard deviation is √2 times the typical error of a single measurement. Dividing by √2 recovers the error of one measurement, which is the noise against which any individual change should be judged.

questions.prompt: A joint-angle measure has a standard error of measurement (SEM) of 1.5°. What is the minimal detectable change at 95% confidence (MDC95) in degrees? Round to two decimal places.
questions.explanation: MDC95 = 1.96 × √2 × SEM. The √2 term reflects that a change score involves two measurements, each with error. A change smaller than about 4.2° in this measure cannot be distinguished from measurement error at 95% confidence for an individual, whatever coaches or software report.

stimulus.text: Two velocity devices are tested against a criterion system. Device A reads on average 3.0 mph high, with a random error SD of 0.3 mph. Device B shows no average bias, with a random error SD of 1.5 mph. (Synthetic values.)

questions.prompt: For tracking each pitcher's own changes across sessions on the same device, which statement is most accurate?

options.text: Device A is better for within-athlete change, because a constant bias cancels in change scores; its bias matters when comparing with other systems or norms
Device B is better for every purpose, because it is unbiased
Both devices are equally useful because their errors average out over a season
Device A is unusable because a biased instrument is never valid

questions.explanation: A constant bias cancels when the same device measures the same athlete twice, so device A's small random error makes it the better tool for detecting individual change. Its bias still matters when its readings are compared with another system or with published norms. Device B is accurate on average but too noisy for small individual changes.

optionFeedback.b: Lack of bias does not compensate for large random error when the goal is detecting small individual changes.
optionFeedback.c: Bias and random error behave differently; random error does not disappear for single-session decisions.
optionFeedback.d: A known constant bias can be corrected or ignored for within-device comparisons; validity depends on the intended use.

stimulus.text: A markerless system is compared with a marker-based system for peak shoulder external rotation in 30 pitchers. The correlation between systems is r = 0.95. The mean difference (markerless minus marker-based) is 2.0°, and the standard deviation of the differences is 3.0°. (Synthetic values.)

questions.prompt: What are the 95% limits of agreement, and what follows?

options.text: About −1.0° to +5.0°; the systems can be used interchangeably because r = 0.95
About −3.9° to +7.9°; despite the high correlation, individual readings can differ by several degrees, so the systems are not interchangeable without considering that range
About −5.9° to +5.9°; there is no systematic bias
Limits of agreement cannot be computed without the raw data; r = 0.95 shows the systems agree

questions.explanation: Limits of agreement are the mean difference ± 1.96 × the SD of the differences: 2.0 ± 5.88, about −3.9° to +7.9°. A high correlation shows that the two systems rank pitchers similarly, not that they agree; a systematic offset and individual differences of several degrees can coexist with r = 0.95. Whether that range is acceptable depends on the size of the changes the users need to detect.

optionFeedback.a: That uses ±1 SD rather than ±1.96 SD, and treats correlation as agreement.
optionFeedback.c: This drops the 2.0° mean difference, which is the systematic bias.
optionFeedback.d: The mean and SD of the differences are exactly what is needed, and correlation is not agreement.

stimulus.text: In a cross-sectional study of 40 pitchers, those with greater peak hip–shoulder separation threw faster (r = 0.45). A report concludes: "Each pitcher who increases his separation will throw harder, so all pitchers should train to increase it." (Synthetic study.)

questions.prompt: What is the most important flaw in the recommendation?

options.text: A correlation of 0.45 is too small to be statistically significant with 40 pitchers
It applies a between-athlete association to within-athlete change and treats correlation as causation
Hip–shoulder separation cannot be measured reliably
The study should have used more than one velocity measure per pitcher

questions.explanation: A between-athlete correlation describes how pitchers differ from one another, not what happens when one pitcher changes. The association may reflect third variables such as body size, strength or skill level, and the within-athlete relationship can differ in size or even direction. Only an intervention design, ideally randomized with retention and transfer tests, can show that changing separation changes velocity.

optionFeedback.a: With n = 40, r = 0.45 is conventionally significant (p ≈ 0.004); significance is not the problem.
optionFeedback.c: Measurement quality matters, but the inferential leap would be invalid even with perfect measurement.
optionFeedback.d: More trials would improve reliability but would not license a causal, within-athlete conclusion.

questions.prompt: A club selects the 10 hitters with the lowest average exit velocity in one week's batting practice for a new drill. The next week their average exit velocity has risen. Which conclusion is most justified?

options.text: The drill works, because every selected hitter improved on average
The drill harmed the other hitters, whose average fell
Some or all of the rise is expected from regression to the mean; a comparable control group is needed to estimate the drill's effect
Exit velocity is too unreliable to measure, so no conclusion is possible about anything

questions.explanation: Hitters chosen for extreme low scores on a noisy measure will, on average, score closer to their true level next time even without any intervention. That is regression to the mean. To isolate the drill's effect you need a comparable control group selected the same way, ideally randomized, and repeated measures.

optionFeedback.a: Improvement after selection on low scores is expected even with no effect.
optionFeedback.b: No data on the other hitters are given, and any fall among high scorers would also reflect regression to the mean.
optionFeedback.d: Imperfect reliability is what produces regression to the mean; it does not make measurement worthless.

questions.prompt: In a study of 16 hitters, the mean change in bat speed is 2.5 mph with a standard deviation of change of 8.0 mph. Using a two-sided t critical value of 2.131 (15 degrees of freedom), what is the half-width of the 95% confidence interval for the mean change, in mph? Round to two decimal places.
questions.explanation: The standard error of the mean is SD / √n, and the half-width is t × SE. The interval runs from about −1.8 to +6.8 mph, so it includes zero as well as large benefits. Small samples with variable responses give very imprecise estimates, which is a common feature of applied biomechanics studies.

questions.prompt: A vendor claims a training program increases bat speed. Rank these forms of evidence from strongest support for a causal effect on lasting bat speed (first) to weakest (last).

options.text: A randomized controlled trial with a control group and a retention test weeks later
A non-randomized study comparing athletes who chose the program with athletes who did not
A single-group pre–post study measured on the program's first and last day
Video testimonials from athletes who used the program

questions.explanation: Random allocation with a control group and delayed retention testing best separates the program's effect from maturation, practice effects, regression to the mean and short-term warm-up effects. A non-randomized comparison group helps but leaves selection bias. A single-group pre–post design cannot separate the program from time and practice. Testimonials select successes and lack any comparison.

optionFeedback.a: Strongest: randomization and retention testing address the main alternative explanations.
optionFeedback.b: A comparison group helps, but self-selection may make groups differ in motivation or ability.
optionFeedback.c: No comparison group, and the last-day measure captures performance rather than retention.
optionFeedback.d: Weakest: selected, uncontrolled and unmeasured.

functional-anatomy.strong: You reason comfortably about moment arms, muscle mechanics and the stretch-shortening cycle. In Week 1, concentrate on how these properties constrain throwing and swinging, and on where the evidence for specific mechanisms is contested.
functional-anatomy.developing: You handle some of the mechanics of muscle and joints but not all of it. Pay attention to the moment-arm calculations and to the force–velocity and length–tension relationships when they appear in Week 1.
functional-anatomy.foundation: Optional refresher before Lesson 1: review lever mechanics and static moment balance about a joint, the length–tension and force–velocity relationships, fiber types, and the stretch-shortening cycle, using the muscle mechanics chapter of a standard biomechanics text. Work two or three static elbow or knee moment problems by hand.

vector-mathematics.strong: Your vector and rotation skills are ready for three-dimensional joint-angle work. In Week 1, focus on the conventions (axis definitions, Cardan sequences) that make published values comparable or not.
vector-mathematics.developing: You are comfortable with parts of vector algebra but less sure of others, often cross products or rotation sequences. Rework the sign conventions and the right-hand rule carefully in Week 1 rather than skimming them.
vector-mathematics.foundation: Optional refresher before Lesson 2: review vector addition, magnitude, the dot product (angles between vectors) and the cross product with the right-hand rule; converting degrees to radians and using v = ωr; and the idea of a rotation matrix and why rotation order matters. An introductory linear algebra or engineering mechanics chapter on vectors covers this; do a handful of hand calculations.

kinematics.strong: You interpret kinematic quantities and their processing well. In Weeks 1 and 2, concentrate on how definitions and filtering choices change the numbers reported for pitching and hitting.
kinematics.developing: You know the main kinematic quantities but some definitions or processing issues are unsettled. Watch the distinction between joint and segment angular velocity, and the role of filtering, when they appear.
kinematics.foundation: Optional refresher before Lesson 2: review position, velocity and acceleration as derivatives, projectile motion without drag, the relation between angular and linear velocity, and why differentiating noisy data requires filtering. A first-year physics kinematics chapter plus a short section on low-pass filtering in a biomechanics methods text is enough.

kinetics.strong: You apply impulse–momentum, joint power and angular momentum correctly and you separate net joint moments from tissue loads. In Week 1, focus on inverse dynamics assumptions and their limits.
kinetics.developing: You handle some kinetic reasoning but not all, often joint power or angular momentum. Work the examples in Lesson 3 step by step, stating sign conventions each time.
kinetics.foundation: Optional refresher before Lesson 3: review Newton's laws in linear and angular form, impulse and momentum, moment of inertia and conservation of angular momentum, and mechanical power as moment times angular velocity. A first-year physics treatment of rotational dynamics plus the inverse dynamics chapter of a biomechanics text covers it.

motor-control.strong: You reason well about redundancy, delays and the difference between performance and learning. In Week 1, focus on the competing theories of motor control and the quality of evidence for each.
motor-control.developing: You recognize some motor control ideas but not all, often optimal feedback control or the role of sensorimotor delay. Read Lesson 5 closely, especially the sections on prediction and on how variability is analyzed.
motor-control.foundation: Optional refresher before Lesson 5: review the degrees-of-freedom problem, feedback versus feedforward control and typical sensorimotor delays, the idea of forward models, and the difference between performance and learning (retention and transfer tests). A motor control textbook's chapters on control theories and motor learning cover this; Course A's learning science week also helps with the last point.

measurement-science.strong: You handle typical error, minimal detectable change and agreement analysis confidently. In Week 2, focus on how these statistics apply to specific systems and on what validation studies did and did not test.
measurement-science.developing: You know some reliability statistics but mix up others, often agreement versus correlation or the √2 in change scores. Work the calculations in Week 2 Lesson 5 by hand.
measurement-science.foundation: Optional refresher before Week 2: review accuracy versus precision, systematic versus random error, the standard error of measurement and typical error, minimal detectable change, intraclass correlation, and Bland–Altman limits of agreement. A measurement chapter in a sports science research methods text covers this; calculate each statistic once from a small made-up test–retest table.

research-literacy.strong: You read study designs critically and separate between- from within-athlete evidence. Throughout the course, apply this to the specific biomechanics literature, where samples are small and most designs are cross-sectional.
research-literacy.developing: You catch some design problems but not all, often regression to the mean or the between- versus within-athlete distinction. Use the evidence tables in each lesson deliberately rather than skipping to conclusions.
research-literacy.foundation: Optional refresher before Week 1: review study designs (cross-sectional, pre–post, controlled and randomized trials), confidence intervals and why small samples give imprecise estimates, regression to the mean, and why correlation does not establish causation. Course A's research methods week, or an introductory research methods text for sport science, covers it.

library.title: Sequential motions of body segments in striking and throwing skills: descriptions and explanations
library.license: Copyright holder's terms. Linked, not reproduced.

library.summary: A review of the proximal-to-distal sequence in striking and throwing. Explaining the sequence requires analysing segment interaction, not only muscle moments.
Differences in interaction between skills should be studied before general principles are stated.

The description provides reference patterns for skilled hitters.

library.license: Copyright holder's terms. Linked, not reproduced.

library.summary: Shows that human estimates of hand position during movement in the dark are consistent with an internal model that combines a forward prediction from motor commands with delayed sensory feedback, in the manner of a Kalman filter.
arguments: The nervous system estimates limb state by combining prediction from motor commands with sensory feedback.
Errors in estimated hand position over the course of a movement follow the pattern predicted by such an observer model.
Internal models offer a way to act despite sensory delays.

library.title: Biomechanics and Motor Control of Human Movement (4th ed.)
library.license: Copyright holder's terms. Linked, not reproduced.

verified.evidence: Title, author, edition, publisher, year and DOI supplied by the course brief as verified in November 2026; rechecked against the Wiley DOI record listed there.

library.summary: The standard graduate textbook on the mechanics of human movement. It develops segment kinematics, anthropometry, link-segment kinetics, inverse dynamics, mechanical work, energy and power, and muscle mechanics, with worked numerical procedures that can be implemented directly.
arguments: Net joint moments and joint reaction forces can be computed from kinematics, segment inertial properties and external forces by solving the link-segment equations from the distal end inward.
A net joint moment is the summed effect of all muscles, ligaments and contact forces crossing the joint; it cannot be partitioned into individual structures without further modelling.
Mechanical power at a joint is the product of the net joint moment and the joint angular velocity, and its sign shows whether the moment is generating or absorbing energy.
library.design: Textbook with derivations and worked examples.
library.strengths: Rigorous, explicit about assumptions (rigid segments, frictionless hinge joints, estimated inertial parameters), and widely used, so its vocabulary matches the research literature.
library.limitations: Examples come mostly from gait and planar analyses; three-dimensional and high-speed sporting applications need extension; the 4th edition predates markerless capture.
library.generalizability: The mechanics are general and apply directly to pitching and hitting; the numerical examples need rescaling to the much higher velocities of throwing and swinging.
library.relevance: Gives you the mechanics behind every joint moment, power and energy value in a biomechanics report, so you can see what was assumed to produce them.

Within-athlete analyses address a different question from between-athlete comparisons.
