library.strengths: Clear statement of the functional-variability view and its measurement.
library.limitations: Much of the evidence comes from gait and clinical populations; the 'optimal' amount is hard to define in advance.
library.contested: The optimal-variability hypothesis is influential but difficult to falsify; see R-bartlett-2007-is for a sport-biomechanics perspective.
library.generalizability: Conceptually relevant to pitching and hitting; quantitative thresholds do not transfer.
library.relevance: Frames variability as information about the system rather than a defect to be removed.

library.title: The Co-ordination and Regulation of Movements
library.license: Copyright holder's terms. Linked, not reproduced.

verified.evidence: Title, author, publisher and 1967 English edition matched in the Texas A&M library catalogue record and Elsevier's description of the 1984 reassessment volume, which reprints the text.

library.summary: A collection of Bernstein's papers translated into English. It frames coordination as the mastery of redundant degrees of freedom and emphasizes that the same goal is achieved by different movements on each repetition.
arguments: The motor system has many more degrees of freedom than any task requires (the degrees-of-freedom problem).
Coordination is the process of mastering redundant degrees of freedom, converting the body into a controllable system.
Repetition without repetition: skilled performers solve the same problem anew rather than reproducing a fixed motion.
library.design: Theoretical and experimental papers from the 1920s–1960s.
library.strengths: Foundational for modern motor control and the study of variability.
library.limitations: Historical; much of the evidence predates modern measurement.
library.generalizability: General to all skilled movement.
library.relevance: The origin of the questions that underlie individual movement solutions in pitching and hitting.

library.title: A survey of formal methods for determining the centre of rotation of ball joints
library.license: Copyright holder's terms. Linked, not reproduced.

verified.evidence: Authors, title, journal, volume, issue, pages and year matched in a University of Southampton repository record and PubMed listing (PMID 16293257). DOI not confirmed in search results and therefore omitted.

library.summary: Compares formal (functional) methods for locating a ball joint's centre of rotation from marker data and introduces a symmetrical method (SCoRE) that does not require one segment to remain stationary.
arguments: Functional methods estimate joint centres from relative segment motion.
Under the test conditions, most methods located the centre within about 0.3 cm when range of motion was at least 45°.
The symmetrical approach allows both segments to move during calibration.
library.design: Simulation and experimental comparison of joint-centre estimation methods.
library.strengths: Formal comparison under controlled conditions.
library.limitations: Accuracy under simulation is an upper bound; soft-tissue artifact during calibration movements degrades real performance.
library.generalizability: Relevant to hip and glenohumeral centres in pitching and hitting models.
library.relevance: Explains the functional versus predictive joint-centre choice.

library.title: Concurrent assessment of gait kinematics using marker-based and markerless motion capture
library.license: Copyright holder's terms. Linked, not reproduced.

verified.evidence: Authors, title, journal, volume, article number and DOI matched in web search (Elsevier Pure record and bioRxiv preprint); findings and the disclosed author conflict from the preprint and abstract.

library.summary: Compared Theia3D markerless and marker-based capture during treadmill walking in 30 adults recorded simultaneously.
arguments: Joint-centre differences were about 2.5 cm or less for most joints and 3.6 cm at the hip.
Joint-angle patterns were similar; rotations about segment long axes differed most.
The authors judged markerless capture a suitable alternative where its practical benefits are preferred.
library.design: Simultaneous 8-camera markerless and 7-camera marker capture of treadmill gait, 30 adults.
library.strengths: Simultaneous capture; clear reporting of joint-centre differences.
library.limitations: Walking is slow and planar compared with throwing; one author led the vendor company.
library.generalizability: Gait agreement is an upper bound for fast throwing and swinging.
library.relevance: Shows where markerless error concentrates (long-axis rotation) in a simpler task.

library.title: Functional and clinical significance of skeletal muscle architecture
library.license: Copyright holder's terms. Linked, not reproduced.

verified.evidence: Title, authors, journal, volume, issue and pages matched in several reference listings and index records (Thieme reference list, unibo index, typeset); DOI not displayed in results, so it is omitted; URL is the DeepDyve listing seen in search.

library.summary: A review of skeletal muscle architecture — fibre length, pennation and physiological cross-sectional area — and why it dominates a muscle's force and excursion capacity, with clinical applications such as tendon transfer.
arguments: Physiological cross-sectional area is the main architectural determinant of maximal isometric force.
Fibre length (number of sarcomeres in series) determines excursion range and maximal shortening velocity.
Architecture differs widely across upper- and lower-limb muscles and should guide clinical and functional interpretation.
library.design: Narrative review of cadaveric architectural data and muscle physiology.
library.strengths: Widely used reference; clear link between structure and function.
library.limitations: Cadaveric architecture data come mainly from older adults; in vivo architecture adapts with training.
library.generalizability: The structure–function principles transfer to athletes; the specific values do not.
library.relevance: Explains why a muscle's design, not only its size, constrains speed and range in throwing and swinging.

library.title: Is movement variability important for sports biomechanists?
library.license: Copyright holder's terms. Linked, not reproduced.

verified.evidence: Title, authors, journal, volume, issue, pages and DOI matched the Sheffield Hallam (SHURA) record and an open post-print at Nottingham Trent University (IRep).

library.summary: Argues that movement variability, long treated by sport biomechanists as noise, is or may be functional; reviews within- and between-individual variability in throwing, basketball shooting and locomotion and notes that even elite performers do not reproduce identical patterns.
arguments: Variability is not solely neuromuscular or measurement noise; some of it may be functional.
Elite athletes do not show motor invariance, which challenges the use of a single 'representative' trial.
Biomechanists should study variability together with coordination and learning.
library.design: Narrative review.
library.strengths: Sport-specific; accessible open post-print; directly addresses practice in biomechanics laboratories.
library.limitations: Selective rather than systematic review.
library.generalizability: Applies directly to how pitching and hitting trials are averaged and interpreted.
library.relevance: A short, sharp argument against reading one 'best' trial as the athlete's movement.

library.title: Effect of Excessive Contralateral Trunk Tilt on Pitching Biomechanics and Performance in High School Baseball Pitchers
library.license: Copyright holder's terms. Linked, not reproduced.

verified.evidence: Citation and DOI supplied by the course brief as verified; 72 high school pitchers, higher ball speed (about 32.6 vs 31.1 m/s) and higher arm kinetics in the excessive-tilt group matched the Georgia Southern repository abstract.

library.summary: Compared high school pitchers with and without excessive contralateral trunk tilt. The tilt group threw faster and also had greater elbow and shoulder forces and moments; the authors called contralateral tilt a strategy associated with both higher ball speed and higher joint loading.
arguments: Contralateral trunk tilt is associated with higher ball speed in high school pitchers.
The same strategy is associated with greater shoulder and elbow loads.
Whether coaches should encourage or discourage it is unresolved.
library.design: Cross-sectional comparison of two groups defined by frontal-view trunk tilt.
library.strengths: Reports performance and loading together.
library.limitations: Cross-sectional; group split on one variable; high school sample.
library.generalizability: High school pitchers; adult magnitudes may differ.
library.relevance: A clean example of a mechanical choice that trades velocity against load.

library.title: An Analysis of In Vivo Hip Kinematics in Elite Baseball Batters Using a Markerless Motion-Capture System
library.license: Open access; copyright holder's terms. Linked, not reproduced.

verified.evidence: Title, journal, first author, year and DOI matched on the Wiley/ScienceDirect listing in web search; sample of 29 elite players and the markerless system (Dynamic Athletic Research Institute) from the abstract. Volume/issue and co-authors not confirmed.

library.summary: Used a markerless system to measure lead- and trail-hip motion during swings in 29 elite baseball players, reporting differences between the two hips.
arguments: Markerless capture was used to describe hip range of motion during batting.
Lead and trail hips differed significantly.
library.design: Cross-sectional descriptive study, 29 elite players.
library.strengths: An early application of markerless capture to hitting.
library.limitations: Small sample; no validation against a marker-based reference reported in the material reviewed.
library.generalizability: Descriptive; not a validation of markerless swing measurement.
library.relevance: Shows the early, descriptive state of markerless hitting research.

library.title: A Guideline of Selecting and Reporting Intraclass Correlation Coefficients for Reliability Research
library.license: Open access via PubMed Central (PMC4913118); copyright holder's terms.

verified.evidence: Title, journal, volume, issue, pages, DOI and PMCID matched in web search (Scilit, GESIS and PMC records); interpretation thresholds from a secondary summary and consistent with the paper's widely cited guidance.

library.summary: Explains the ten forms of ICC defined by model, type and definition, recommends reporting each choice with confidence intervals, and offers interpretation thresholds based on the confidence interval.
arguments: ICC form depends on model (one-way random, two-way random, two-way mixed), type (single or mean) and definition (agreement or consistency).
Report software, model, type, definition and the 95% confidence interval.
Values below 0.5 indicate poor, 0.5–0.75 moderate, 0.75–0.9 good and above 0.9 excellent reliability.
library.design: Methodological guideline.
library.strengths: Practical, explicit reporting checklist.
library.limitations: Thresholds are conventions, not decision rules for individuals.
library.generalizability: Applies to all reliability studies in biomechanics.
library.relevance: Reference for reading ICCs in validation papers.

library.title: Comparison of kinematic and temporal parameters between different pitch velocity groups
library.license: Copyright holder's terms. Linked, not reproduced.

verified.evidence: Citation and DOI supplied by the course brief as verified; design (12 kinematic and 9 temporal parameters, high- and low-velocity groups from 127 college and professional pitchers) and principal findings matched abstract excerpts in index records.

library.summary: Compared high- and low-velocity groups drawn from 127 college and professional pitchers. The high-velocity group showed greater maximum shoulder external rotation, more forward trunk tilt at release and greater lead-knee extension velocity at release; the low-velocity group showed greater lead-knee flexion velocity.
arguments: Several kinematic variables differ between pitchers who throw harder and those who throw softer.
Greater shoulder external rotation lengthens the acceleration path.
Lead-knee behaviour differs between velocity groups.
library.design: Cross-sectional comparison of extreme velocity groups.
library.strengths: Large sample for its era; explicit group contrast.
library.limitations: Between-pitcher comparison of extreme groups inflates apparent differences; does not show that changing a variable changes velocity.
library.generalizability: College and professional pitchers; associations only.
library.relevance: A classic example of between-athlete differences that are easily misread as coaching targets.

library.title: Trends Supporting the In-Field Use of Wearable Inertial Sensors for Sport Performance Evaluation: A Systematic Review
library.license: Open access (MDPI); copyright holder's terms. Linked, not reproduced.

verified.evidence: Authors, title, journal, volume, article number and DOI matched on PubMed Central (PMC5877384) and university repositories in web search; review scope from the abstract.

library.summary: A systematic review of wearable inertial sensors in sport (286 studies and 23 reviews to April 2017), covering capacity assessment, technique analysis, activity classification and physical demands.
arguments: Most in-field IMU studies were conducted in training rather than competition.
Technique analysis was the most common application.
Reliability of sensor-based indicators and calibration remain central concerns.
library.design: Systematic search of four databases to April 2017.
library.strengths: Broad, systematic coverage of in-field IMU use.
library.limitations: Search ends in 2017; heterogeneous studies limit quantitative synthesis.
library.generalizability: Principles apply to baseball wearables; few included studies concern throwing or batting.
library.relevance: Frames what IMUs measure and why field reliability must be shown.

library.title: Measures of reliability in sports medicine and science
library.license: Author-hosted copy at sportsci.org; copyright holder's terms. Linked, not reproduced.

verified.evidence: Title, author, journal, volume, issue, pages and DOI supplied in the brief and matched on the DOI resolver and Victoria University repository in web search; author-hosted PDF on sportsci.org.

library.summary: Argues that the typical error of measurement — within-subject standard deviation, often expressed as a coefficient of variation — should be the main reliability statistic in sport science, alongside change in the mean and retest correlation.
arguments: Reliability has three components: within-subject random variation, systematic change in the mean, and retest correlation.
The typical error is the standard deviation of an individual's repeated measurements.
For two trials, typical error equals the SD of difference scores divided by √2.
library.design: Methodological review with worked statistics.
library.strengths: Practical, widely used framework.
library.limitations: Some recommendations (e.g., log transformation) need judgement for angular data.
library.generalizability: Directly applicable to biomechanical monitoring.
library.relevance: The basis of this week's typical-error and MDC calculations.

glossary.definition: An origin and three perpendicular unit vectors used to express positions and orientations; global frames are fixed to the laboratory, segment frames move with a body segment.
The orientation of one segment frame relative to another, expressed as three rotations under a stated sequence and axis convention.
A decomposition of orientation into three rotations about three different axes (for example Z–X–Y); singular when the middle rotation reaches ±90°.
A decomposition in which the first and third rotations are about the same axis (for example Y–X–Y, the ISB humeral sequence); singular at a middle rotation of 0° or 180°.
A singular orientation of a rotation sequence at which two axes align, only the sum or difference of two angles is defined, and reported angles become unstable.
The vector rate of rotation of a segment, in rad/s; in 3D it is not, in general, the time derivative of a reported joint angle.
The time integral of force (area under the force–time curve, N·s), equal to the change in linear momentum when net of all other forces.
The rotational effect of a force about an axis, M = r × F, with magnitude equal to force times moment arm and direction given by the right-hand rule.
For a rigid segment about a principal axis, I·ω; total angular momentum about the centre of mass changes only through external moments.
The time integral of moment (N·m·s), equal to the change in angular momentum.
The resultant moment at a joint computed by inverse dynamics; the sum of the contributions of all muscles, ligaments and contact forces, not the load on any one structure.
Computing net joint forces and moments from measured motion, estimated segment inertial properties and external forces, segment by segment.
Net joint moment multiplied by joint angular velocity; positive values generate mechanical energy, negative values absorb it.
A moment on a segment produced by the motion (especially the velocity) of linked segments rather than by muscles crossing its joint.
The common pattern in which segments from the pelvis outward reach peak angular velocity in order, each distal peak typically higher than the last.
Quantifying mechanical power moving between segments through joint forces and segment torques, computed from inverse-dynamics outputs.
Posterior twisting of the humeral head relative to the elbow axis; greater on the throwing side of experienced throwers, shifting the rotational arc toward external rotation.
The sum of passive internal and external rotation at the glenohumeral joint, usually compared between the throwing and non-throwing sides.
The decline in a muscle's force as its shortening speed increases, and the increase in force above isometric when it is forcibly lengthened.
Tendon, aponeurosis and other passive tissue in series with muscle fibres, able to store strain energy when stretched and return it quickly.
The availability of many joint and muscle combinations that achieve the same task outcome; the basis of Bernstein's degrees-of-freedom problem.
The set of joint configurations that leave a chosen task variable unchanged; variance along it is task-irrelevant, variance across it changes the outcome.
Organismic, environmental and task constraints whose interaction shapes the coordination pattern a performer uses.
A sphere coated to reflect infrared light back toward its source, whose 3D position an optical system reconstructs by triangulation from two or more cameras.
Motion of skin-mounted markers relative to the underlying bone caused by skin sliding, muscle deformation and inertial effects; the dominant error in marker-based bone kinematics.
A joint centre estimated from the relative motion of two segments, for example by fitting the centre of the spheres traced by markers about a ball joint.
A joint centre located from palpated anatomical landmarks using regression equations derived from reference samples.
A method for choosing a low-pass filter cut-off by examining the RMS difference between raw and filtered signals across cut-off frequencies.
Detection of body keypoints in images by a trained neural network; in multi-camera systems the 2D detections are combined into a 3D skeletal model.
A point a pose-estimation model is trained to locate in an image, such as a visual estimate of the elbow; not necessarily an anatomical joint centre.
An index of similarity between waveforms across a movement cycle; largely insensitive to constant offsets between curves.
The average 3D distance between corresponding joint positions estimated by two systems, a screening metric for markerless accuracy.
The point of application of the resultant ground reaction force on a force plate, computed from the plate's moments divided by vertical force.
The time integral of force, equal to the change in momentum it produces; measured in newton-seconds.
Combining gyroscope, accelerometer and sometimes magnetometer signals to estimate orientation while correcting drift with gravity or magnetic references.
Orientation error that accumulates when angular velocity containing a bias is integrated over time.
A smoothed amplitude profile of an EMG signal obtained by full-wave rectification followed by low-pass filtering.
Expressing EMG amplitude relative to a reference, such as a maximal voluntary isometric contraction or the task peak, so that amplitudes can be compared.
Half the sampling rate; signal content above it cannot be represented and aliases to lower frequencies.
The vertical direction in which the bat's sweet spot is travelling at contact, as defined by MLB's Statcast bat-tracking glossary.
The speed of the bat's sweet spot at contact, or where contact would have occurred on a miss, as defined by MLB's Statcast glossary.
The standard deviation of an individual's repeated measurements; from two trials, the SD of difference scores divided by √2.
The smallest change in an individual that exceeds measurement error with 95% confidence: 1.96 × √2 × typical error.
The proportion of total variance due to differences between subjects; its value depends on the model, type, definition and the sample's heterogeneity.
In a Bland–Altman analysis, the mean difference between methods plus or minus 1.96 standard deviations of the differences.
